events.text: A thousand days without harm, and all the years after them. Tonight, on the grave mound where you first bowed to the moon, something opens behind you like a fan being shaken out. You do not need to turn round. You can feel it the way you feel your own breath: the ninth tail, and the tip of it as white as frost. The moon looks at it for a long time, the way a creditor looks at an account that has come out right.

choices.text: Lift all nine tails to the moon, once, where the whole valley can see

effects.log: Nine tails of pale fire stand up on the hill above the paddies for the space of one breath. In the village a dog howls, and a grandmother at a window says the name of every fox story she ever heard, in order.

choices.text: Fold them away at once. A tail is one more thing to hide

effects.log: You fold the ninth with the other eight, the way you folded the first. The vixen who bore you told you to count your own tails and never hers. You count. Nine. Then you never count them again in the open.

choices.text: Go down to the earth under the mound and lie there till dawn

effects.log: The earth under the grave mound is the size of a wardrobe now, and you are the size of a hill pony. You lie with your nose at the entrance and your tails out on the frost. Pine roots, soil, the old dead. Home, a little crowded.

events.text: The ninth tail opens on a night with no moon, which is the only kind of night it could. You feel it come the way you felt every borrowed breath go into the bead: warm, quick, and not yours. In the black water of a flooded paddy you look at it. It is as long and fine as the other eight, and darker at the root, as if it had been dipped in something. You know exactly what.

choices.text: Sit by the water and count the pale faces it grew on

effects.log: Sleepers in lamplit rooms, one after another: one with ink on the cuffs, one who sold chestnuts, one who sang in the fields. You count until the frogs stop. It does not make the root of the tail any lighter. It makes you a fox who knows the number.

choices.text: Tell yourself a tail is only a tail

effects.log: It is a fine tail. It is a very fine tail. You walk home with it held high, and the dogs of four villages lose their voices for a week.

choices.text: Go at once and give one breath back

effects.log: Before dawn you are at the window of a house where somebody has been pale for a year. The bead goes on your breath, for a night, and comes back. One. The ledger is very long, and that was one.

events.text: Nine tails, and the whole mountain wakes up to it. The deer stop at the edge of your hill and do not cross it. The owls in the pine move to another pine. A badger brings a dead pheasant to the mouth of your earth and backs away, as if paying rent. And at noon, on the bare rock where the mountain's old spirit is said to sit, there is a single pine cone laid very straight, which was not there yesterday.

choices.text: Leave the pheasant for the badger, and a pine cone of your own beside the first

effects.log: The next day both pine cones are gone and there is a smooth white stone in their place. Something old on this mountain has decided to be polite to you. Politeness, at your age, is the beginning of most things.

choices.text: Walk the whole mountain by night so everything knows whose it is

effects.log: Ridge, gully, spring, spring, ridge. By dawn there is not a creature on the mountain that has not smelled foxfire. The badger moves out. The pine cones stop. You have the mountain, and nobody to share it with.

choices.text: Lie low a season and let the mountain get used to you

effects.log: You let the deer come back across your hill, and pretend not to see them. By spring a hare is grazing on your grave mound. Nine tails, and a hare is not afraid of you. You are prouder of that than of the tails.

events.text: A board is nailed up outside the county office, and copied, and nailed up outside two more: a bounty for the nine-tailed fox of the grave-mound hill, in rice, with a description. The description is wrong in almost every particular. It is right about the tails. The fox hunters of three provinces, who have never agreed on anything, have agreed on you.

choices.text: Read it at night, closely, and learn what they think you look like

effects.log: They think you are white all over, with red eyes, and the height of a horse. You will make a point of being none of those things. A wrong description is a gift, if you are careful with it.

choices.text: Lead the first hunting party round the same hill until they go home

ok.log: Three days. Foxfire on the left, foxfire on the right, the same pine three times an afternoon. On the fourth morning the hunters sit down by the road and eat their rice in silence and walk home. The bounty board gets a second line: difficult.

fail.log: One of them is a hunter of the old kind, who does not follow lights. An arrow takes a hand's breadth of fur off your flank. You get away. They now know your colour. (-12 health)

choices.text: Sleep a year under the mound and let the board weather

effects.log: Rain on the board, sun on the board, a goat that eats the corner of the board. By autumn the bounty is a joke the children tell, and nobody remembers the description.

events.text: A thousand years. You do not mark it; the bead marks it for you. One morning it is simply full: not bright, not glowing, full, the way a jar is full, so that one more drop of moonlight would run over. You open your mouth in the dawn and the light comes out of it and lies on the frost. You can be anyone now. Not a crude face with the ears left on: anyone, down to the way they cough.

choices.text: Wear no face at all for a whole year, to remember your own

effects.log: A year as a fox, only a fox, with a full bead in its mouth and nothing to pretend. It is the strangest year of your life. You catch voles. You are terrible at it now.

choices.text: Wear, for one evening, the face of someone dead whom you loved

ok.log: You get it exactly: the way they held a cup, the joke they always started and never finished. You sit in it on the mound until moonset. Then you put it away carefully, and do not wear it again. Some faces are for remembering, not for wearing.

fail.log: You get it almost right, and almost is worse than wrong. You sit in a face that is not quite theirs and grieve for the difference, and put it away before dawn. (-5 health)

choices.text: Wear the face of the salt peddler who chased your kind for three generations

effects.log: You walk the hill road at dusk in a salt peddler's face with an A-frame on your back, and every fox on the hill goes flat in the grass as you pass. You laugh all the way home. It is a very good face. You understand, at last, why they always looked so calm.

events.text: The full bead talks, a little, the way a full jar hums when the wind crosses its mouth. It says three things over and over, on the full-moon nights. A house, and a name of your own, and cold feet in the morning. A mountain that would take you as its spirit, and a pine to lie under. A road of moonlight going up. It does not say which. The old tales never say which. That is the one thing the fox always has to choose alone.

choices.text: Listen hardest to the house and the name

effects.log: You walk past the village at dusk and look in at every lit window, and think: one of those, with no tails behind it. The old rule is still there, waiting: a thousand days without harm, and then a hundred more unseen. Some roads are walked in days.

choices.text: Listen hardest to the mountain

effects.log: You lie under the big pine at the top of the hill and feel the mountain under you breathe, very slowly, once a season. It would take you. It wants something first. Mountains always want a promise.

choices.text: Listen hardest to the road of moonlight

effects.log: You sit up all night with your face to the moon until you can almost see the road: a pale line of cloud, very long, very steep. Heaven reads ledgers. Yours will have to be clean.

choices.text: Refuse to choose yet. You have time

effects.log: A thousand-year fox has exactly one thing in abundance. You spend some of it. The bead goes on humming its three things, patiently, like a teacher who knows you will get there.

events.text: You go over the pass to the next valley, where your aunt Banya kept a house for longer than any village remembers, and find her grave. It is a human grave, a small round mound on a south slope with a stone in front, and on the stone there is a human name and a date. The grandchildren of the family she kept are cutting the grass on it for Chuseok, and arguing, and laughing. Nobody alive knows whether she got her hundred days.

choices.text: Ask the grave

effects.log: Graves do not answer. But the grass on this one is very green and the stone faces the morning, and the family that cuts it has her laugh. You decide that is an answer. It is the one she would have given, anyway: make up your own mind.

choices.text: Help the grandchildren cut the grass, in a passing stranger's face

effects.log: A stranger on the road stops to help with the sickles and knows exactly how the old woman liked her grave. The youngest asks how. "She was my aunt," you say, which is true, and which the family will puzzle over for three generations.

choices.text: Leave a rice cake on a leaf by the stone, the way the mourners did for you

effects.log: One rice cake on a clean leaf, a little apart from the others. The family notices, and leaves one there every year after, and does not know why. Neither, entirely, do you.

events.text: The grave mound you were born under is gone. Not dug up: worn down. A thousand years of rain have made it a low hump in a field of millet, and the family that cut its grass has moved to the capital or died out, and a farmer ploughs round it out of habit without knowing why. The earth underneath has fallen in. You stand where the entrance was. It comes up to your knee.

choices.text: Dig it out again, one night, for no reason

effects.log: You dig until dawn with paws that could open a hillside, very carefully, and make an earth the size of the one you were born in. Too small for you. You put a pine cone in it, for the smallest kit, the one the owl took. Then you go.

choices.text: Ask the farmer, in a face, why he ploughs round it

effects.log: "My grandfather said there is a fox in it," the farmer says. "A lucky one. You do not plough a lucky fox." You thank him gravely. He has no idea how right his grandfather was, a thousand years too late.

choices.text: Leave it to the millet

effects.log: Some places should be allowed to stop being places. You watch the millet move over it for an afternoon and then walk back up the hill, the long way, the way the vixen who bore you taught you.

events.text: A thousand years, and the hunters' bounty boards still say red. Your coat does not. One winter it simply goes pale, from the tail-tips inward, as if frost had been allowed to settle and stay: silver at the tips, white at the chest, a moon-coloured fox. The village dogs, which have barked at you for a thousand years, now lie down flat when you pass and put their chins on their paws.

choices.text: Keep the white. It is what a thousand years looks like

effects.log: Every fur trader in three provinces dreams of a white fox, and every governor's collar is cold. You will be careful. You are always careful. But you will not be red again for anyone.

choices.text: Dye a mask of red over it with the bead, every day, as the price of peace

effects.log: Every morning a little bead-light goes into looking like an ordinary red fox. It is a tax, and you pay it, and the hunters go on looking for the wrong colour.

choices.text: Go and lie down beside the dogs

effects.log: You lie down in the yard among four village dogs who have barked at your family for a thousand years, and they put their heads on your back and sleep. The vixen who bore you would not believe it. You are not sure you do.

events.text: {npc} has lived under one roof with your borrowed face for years: shared the rice, mended the roof with you, argued about the price of salt. {npc} loves the person you pretend to be, the way people love the ones they keep house with, without speeches. And the old rule is there, the last of them, the one the old foxes whisper: a hundred nights under one roof with someone who loves you, and on not one of them may they see you sleep. The full-moon nights are the only nights a fox's sleep shows. So the old foxes count the hundred in full moons.

choices.text: Ask {npc} for it: "For a hundred full moons, do not look at me while I sleep"

mem.note: asked me never to look on full-moon nights

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long moment and then laughs. "Is that all? People ask stranger things." Then, seeing your face: "All right. A hundred. I promise." You have heard a great many promises in all your years. You find you believe this one.

choices.text: Tell {npc} everything first, the tails and all, and then ask

mem.note: told me what it was, and asked me not to look

ok.log: It takes the whole night. {npc} goes white, then red, then silent, then asks one question: "Were you ever unkind to me?" No. "Then a hundred full moons is nothing," says {npc}. "I have not looked at the moon properly in years anyway."

fail.log: You get as far as the tails. {npc} gets up very carefully, walks out of the house, and sits under the persimmon tree until dawn. In the morning {npc} comes back in and makes the rice and does not speak of it. Not now, then. Perhaps not ever.

choices.text: Not yet. Centuries can wait a little longer

effects.log: You let the year go by in the ordinary way: rice, roof, salt. The rule will still be there. So, you hope, will {npc}.

events.text: {npc} has kept house with your borrowed face longer than anyone alive can remember, and is grey now, and still makes the soup the way the family always made it. Tonight, shelling beans, {npc} says without looking up: "You asked me once, a long time ago, not to look at you while you slept. I never asked why. Is it time I did?" And the old rule is there, the last of them: a hundred full moons under one roof, unseen, and a fox may wake human.

choices.text: Ask {npc} for the hundred full moons, now, plainly

effects.log: {npc} puts down the beans. "A hundred," {npc} says. "At my age that is a promise to live eight more years. Very well. I promise that too." You laugh, and then you do not, and {npc} takes your hand across the beans.

choices.text: Ask it of {npc}, who already knows what you are

effects.log: "Tails and all," {npc} says. "I have not looked in years. A hundred more moons is nothing." It is not nothing. It is the most anyone has ever promised you.

choices.text: Not yet. Let the beans be beans

effects.log: "Not yet," you say. {npc} nods, as if that were an answer, and it is. The rule will keep. You are less sure that {npc} will, and that is the whole trouble with people.

events.text: The first full moon. You go to the inner room early and say you have a headache, which is what you will say ninety-nine more times. Through the paper door you can hear {npc} in the outer room, moving the lamp further away, and then further, until it is out on the step. Then the sound of someone sitting down with their back to the door, the way a guard sits.

choices.text: Sleep, and trust the back against the door

effects.log: You sleep. Your tails come out in your sleep, all nine, and lie across the floor like spilled silk, and nobody sees them. In the morning {npc} is asleep on the step with the cold lamp beside them. One.

choices.text: Lie awake listening to {npc} keep watch

effects.log: All night: a cough, a shift, a moth at the lamp, someone humming very quietly so as not to fall asleep. It is the most anyone has done for you in all your years. You do not sleep, so the night does not count. You find you do not mind.

events.text: The thirtieth full moon. A neighbour has noticed, and stops {npc} at the well, and says loudly enough for the whole lane: "Your housemate is never well when the moon is full. My grandmother used to say what that means." {npc} says, "Your grandmother said a great many things," and carries the water home, and does not look at you while setting it down.

choices.text: Ask {npc} whether the neighbour's words stayed

effects.log: "They stayed," {npc} says. "Words do. So does a promise." That is all. You both go back to shelling beans, and the beans have never been so interesting.

choices.text: Bring the neighbour a jar of your best pickles and a long conversation

effects.log: Three hours, two jars, the neighbour's whole family history. By the end the neighbour has decided you are the most respectable person in the lane, and that grandmothers say a great many things.

choices.text: Hide the tails harder: no lamps in the house on moon nights

effects.log: The house goes dark on full-moon nights now, all of it. {npc} sits out on the step in the moonlight instead, and says the moon is better company than a lamp anyway.

events.text: The sixtieth full moon. A salt peddler asks for a night's lodging at the gate, with an A-frame and a forked stick, and there is no inn for ten li. {npc} looks at you. It is the custom to give a traveller a corner. It has always been the custom. The vixen who bore you had a rule about salt peddlers, long ago.

choices.text: Give the peddler the outer room, and sleep anyway

ok.log: The peddler sleeps like a stone and leaves at dawn, and on the way out stops at your inner door, and looks at it, and leaves a small packet of salt on the step. "For the house," the peddler tells {npc}. You never know how much the peddler knew.

fail.log: In the night the stick knocks once, very softly, against your paper door. Nothing more. At dawn the peddler is gone and the whole lane is talking. {npc} says nothing, and keeps the hundred.

choices.text: Send {npc} to put the peddler up at the headman's house

effects.log: It is not quite the custom, and the lane notices. But you sleep. {npc} sits on the step all night anyway, and in the morning says the peddler asked a great many questions about foxes, and was told a great many lies.

choices.text: Stay awake all night in the dark, so there is nothing to see

effects.log: You sit upright in the inner room until dawn with all nine tails folded under you like a cushion. The peddler sleeps. The night does not count. The hundred grows a little longer, and you are a little older.

events.text: The ninetieth full moon, and {npc} is ill: a cough that started at harvest and has gone down into the chest. The physician from the market leaves medicine and a face that says the rest. You lie in the inner room with the full bead in your mouth and listen to the cough through the door, and you know exactly what a night of the bead would do for those lungs. To lend it, you would have to be beside {npc}, awake, with your mouth full of light.

choices.text: Lend the bead, tonight, and let what happens happen

effects.log: You go out through the paper door with the light in your mouth and kneel by the mat. {npc} is too fevered to see anything but a lamp. The bead passes on your breath and comes back. By morning the cough is a cough again. You did not sleep, so the night is not counted. It was not the night that mattered.

choices.text: Fetch the best physician in three counties, in a borrowed hurry

ok.log: Two days on the road there and back. The physician is good, and grumpy, and right. By the end of the month {npc} is sitting up complaining about the food, which is how you know.

fail.log: The first physician is out. The next is drunk. You come home with nothing but sore feet, and find {npc} sitting up, thinner, better, and cross that you went. Luck, this time. Not you. (-8 health)

events.text: The ninety-ninth full moon. The next will be the hundredth. You go into the inner room at dusk with your headache, as always, and lie down. Outside, {npc} takes the lamp out to the step, as always. And then does not sit down. Through the paper you can see the shape of a hand on the frame of the door, holding it, not opening it. All the old stories go through you at once: the one who looked, one day short.

choices.text: Sleep. Trust {npc}

ok.log: You close your eyes. The hand stays on the frame for a long time. Then it goes, and you hear {npc} sit down on the step with a sigh like someone setting down a heavy load. You sleep, tails and all, and nobody sees.

fail.log: You close your eyes. In your sleep the tails come out. And at the hour before dawn the door slides open the width of one eye, and the lamplight comes in across nine tails on the floor, and stops, and the door slides shut again very gently. You wake knowing.

choices.text: Sleep, knowing that {npc} already knows what you are

effects.log: {npc} has known for years, and promised anyway. The hand on the frame is only a hand on a frame: someone steadying themselves to sit down for the last long watch. You sleep like a kit in the earth.

choices.text: Stay awake till dawn so there is nothing to see

effects.log: You lie with your eyes open and your tails held in, and the hand stays on the door all night, and neither of you moves. At dawn it goes. The night is not counted. The ninety-ninth is still to come, and both of you know it now.

events.text: The ninety-ninth full moon, again. Since the night you lay awake, {npc} has not sat on the step at all on moon nights, and has gone to stay with a cousin in the next village every full moon, with an excuse so bad it is almost a confession. Tonight there is no cousin. {npc} is home, in the outer room, and the lamp is lit.

choices.text: Sleep this time, whatever happens

ok.log: The lamp goes out early. You hear {npc} lie down on the far side of the outer room with face to the wall, very deliberately, like a child playing a game of not-looking. You sleep. The ninety-ninth is counted.

fail.log: You sleep. Near dawn a cough wakes {npc}, and in the half-dark {npc} reaches for the water, and the door is open a crack, and the moon is on the floor of the inner room, on your tails. Nobody meant it. That is how it always happens, in the stories.

choices.text: Go and sit with {npc} in the outer room instead, and talk till morning

effects.log: No sleep, no counting. You talk about the roof, the price of salt, the cousin who does not exist. At dawn {npc} says, "Next month, then," and you say, "Next month." Some promises are kept by being put off.

events.text: The hundredth full moon has come and gone, unseen. On the hundred-and-first morning you wake before {npc} does, and something is wrong with your feet. They are cold. You lie under the quilt and work it out slowly: cold, because there are no tails across them. You reach behind you and there is nothing there at all. The bead in your mouth is a small smooth stone, warm, and very quiet.

choices.text: Not yet. Spit the stone into your palm and give the morning back

effects.log: You open your hand and the stone in it lights again, slowly, like a coal blown on. The tails come back across your feet, warm. You lie there with your heart going hard. You could have. Something on the mountain is not finished with you yet, and you are not finished with it.

choices.text: Get up, light the fire, and wake {npc} with a human name that is yours

effects.log: You tell {npc} your name, the one you chose in the night. {npc} says it back twice, getting it right the second time, and asks what you want for breakfast. You will live one life after this, and grow old, and nobody in that house will ever know. It is the best morning of all your years.

events.text: {npc} looked. Neither of you says so. At breakfast {npc} puts the rice down in front of you, and sits, and cannot lift the spoon, and at last says only: "One more night. It was one more night, wasn't it?" The old tales all end here, the same way, with a fox who takes no revenge.

choices.text: Stay, as what you are, if {npc} will have a fox in the house

ok.log: {npc} looks at you a long time, at the tails you do not bother to hide, and then pushes the bowl of rice an inch nearer. "Eat," {npc} says. "You are no good to anyone hungry." No hundred days, no human name. A house, and someone in it who knows. It is not nothing. It may be most of it.

fail.log: {npc} cannot. Not yet; maybe not ever. You go up to the mountain for a season so the house can breathe. When you come down, the lane has a story about a fox, and {npc} tells it worst of all, on purpose, so nobody believes it.

choices.text: Ask {npc} why, without anger

effects.log: "I was afraid you were dying," {npc} says. "You made a sound in your sleep. I only meant to see." It is the reason in half the old tales, too: not doubt, but love that could not wait one more night. You cannot blame it. The hundred will have to begin again, if it ever does.

choices.text: Go back to the mountain, and leave the house everything you had

effects.log: You put a bowl of your best things on the shelf by the ancestral tablets and walk up the hill road in the morning with nine tails behind you in plain sight. {npc} stands in the gate and does not call out. The house is lucky for two hundred years, and nobody can say why.

events.text: The hundredth. Ninety-nine sleepers in ninety-nine villages have grown pale and blamed the spring. You sit beside {npc} in the dark and draw the thread of breath, and the bead comes back warm on it, and then {npc} opens their eyes. Not a dream. Awake, completely, the way the hundredth always wakes in the old stories. {npc} looks at the light at your lips and says, very quietly, "Oh. It is you. It was always you."

choices.text: Close your mouth on the light and go out of the window

effects.log: You are over the wall before the shout. Behind you the whole house wakes, and then the lane, and then the dogs. By morning a hundred people know there is a fox, and one of them knows its face.

choices.text: Stay, and tell {npc} the whole count, all ninety-nine

ok.log: {npc} listens to the end without calling anyone. Ninety-nine faces, ninety-nine villages. At the end {npc} says, "And I am the hundredth." Yes. "Then I will decide what the hundredth does," {npc} says. "Later." You go out through the door, not the window.

fail.log: You get as far as the third name before {npc} screams. You do not blame them. You are out of the window with the house waking behind you, and the count in your mouth like a stone.

choices.text: Let {npc} take it. The old story ends with the hundredth holding the bead

effects.log: {npc} reaches out, quite gently, and takes the bead from the air between you, and swallows it, and falls back on the mat with eyes full of the earth. You are only a fox. An old one. You go out of the window on four ordinary legs, with one ordinary tail.

events.text: Some years on, {npc} walks the hill road at dusk with a schoolmaster's yellow dog on a rope and a book of the old tales under one arm, looking at every stranger. Not to kill a fox: {npc} has told the whole county that much. "I want to ask it something," {npc} says at every gate. "It knows what."

choices.text: Meet {npc} on the hill road in a borrowed face, and let the dog decide

ok.log: The yellow dog sniffs your hand, sneezes, and lies down. {npc} looks at the dog, then at you, then laughs for the first time in a long while. "Walk with me," {npc} says. "Not too close."

fail.log: The dog goes mad. {npc} holds it back with both hands and says, very clearly, over the barking: "Next full moon. The rock in the common graveyard. Come as you are." You go. You would always have gone.

choices.text: Leave the county for a generation

effects.log: You go over three passes and keep a herb stall in a town where nobody has heard of the school road. Somewhere behind you {npc} grows older, asking every stranger the same question. You know what it is. You are not ready.

choices.text: Leave one red-brown hair on the step of the school, where {npc} will find it

effects.log: {npc} finds it at dawn and holds it up to the light for a long time. That evening there is a bowl of rice on the step, and beside it a note in a careful hand: I am not angry. I want to know why.

events.text: The rock in the common graveyard, where the fox of the old story hid. {npc} is waiting, older, with the book of tales open on one knee. "In every version," {npc} says, "the hundredth ends up holding the bead. That is the point of the story. The fox does not get to climb to heaven on a hundred stolen breaths. So." {npc} holds out an open hand.

choices.text: Lend it instead: one night, to see what it sees, and then give it back

ok.log: {npc} holds the bead one night and sees the earth to the bottom: every vein of qi, every grave, every pale face of the ninety-nine. At dawn {npc} gives it back on a breath. "Pay them," {npc} says. "All of them. Then we are even."

fail.log: {npc} will not take a loan from a fox. You argue until the moon sets. In the end {npc} closes the book and walks home, and you are left on the rock with the bead in your mouth and the count still in it. (-10 health)

choices.text: Refuse, and swear to give back every breath before you climb anything

effects.log: "Ninety-nine," {npc} says. "I will be counting." You believe it. For the rest of that life a letter comes every spring to the rock in the graveyard, unsigned, asking only: how many left?

choices.text: Put the bead in the open hand

effects.log: It goes from your mouth to the palm like a drop of the moon. {npc} closes the hand on it and looks, not at the sky, not at the earth, but at you, a long time. You are an ordinary fox again. You live out your years in the ditch by the school road, listening to {npc} teach.

events.text: {npc} is old now, and keeps the village school, and teaches the children one thing before the Thousand Characters: never play games with a stranger on the hill road, however kind, however fine the evening. The children chant it. You lie under the raised floor of the schoolroom, where you learned your letters long ago, and listen.

choices.text: Listen to the end of the lesson, as you did when you were young

effects.npcPass: old age, at the village school, in the middle of a lesson
effects.log: {npc} dies that winter in the middle of the Thousand Characters, between heaven and earth. On the step the next morning there is a rice ball wrapped in a leaf, left by a child who was told to leave one for the stray under the floor.

choices.text: Sit at the back in a borrowed face, and be taught

effects.npcPass: old age, at the village school, smiling at a pupil in the back row
effects.log: {npc} looks at the new pupil in the back row for a long moment and goes on with the lesson, word perfect: never play games with strangers. At the end of the day, passing you, {npc} says only, "Good. You listened."

events.text: There is a rich house at the mouth of the valley with three grown sons, and for nine years the mother of it has climbed your hill to the little shrine stone with rice and a candle, and prayed the same prayer, louder every year: one more child, a last one, even if it is a fox. It is the oldest prayer in the oldest story, and you know how that story goes. Tonight, for the first time, you notice that the prayer is addressed to you.

choices.text: Answer it. A fox can be the child a house prays for, for a while

effects.log: In the spring there is a new child in the rich house, red-haired, quick, laughing, the image of the mother's prayer. The whole valley comes to see. You sit in the cradle of a borrowed childhood and look up at a mother's face, and you are hungry, very slightly, all the time.

choices.text: Tell the mother the old story, in a pedlar's face, at the gate

effects.log: "Even a fox," you say, "and the cattle die one by one, and the son who sees it is driven out, and in the end the house is ash." The mother goes pale and stops praying. Next year she adopts a niece instead, a plain cheerful girl who is not a fox at all.

choices.text: Let the prayer go unanswered

effects.log: Prayers are not orders. The candle burns down on the shrine stone every spring for three more years, and then stops. You feel its absence for a long time, the way you feel a tooth that is gone.

events.text: You are the last child of the house, the one it prayed for, and the house adores you. And every morning, in the cowshed, one cow is found lying cold on the straw with no mark on it. The hired men say ghosts. The youngest son says the cows die of looking at the moon. The eldest son, who sits up one night in the hayloft, says nothing at breakfast, and looks at you over his rice for a long time.

choices.text: Go to the shed on the moon nights anyway. The hunger is very old

effects.log: One cow, then another. You do not remember the nights clearly, which is the worst of it. The eldest son tells the father what he saw from the hayloft, and the father, who prayed for nine years for you, drives his own son out of the gate with a stick.

choices.text: Bind yourself to the house with the vow, and starve politely

effects.log: The cattle live. You grow thin, and pale, and the mother sends for physicians who find nothing. The eldest son stops watching you. Once, in the yard, he brings you a bowl of beef broth without a word. Years later, when he cannot bear not knowing, he leaves the house anyway, to learn what to do about you. (-10 health)

choices.text: Leave the house before anything else dies

effects.log: One morning the prayed-for child is gone from the little bed, and there is a red-brown hair on the pillow. The mother grieves for a year. The cattle live. The eldest son, of all of them, is the one who leaves rice on the shrine stone afterwards.

events.text: {npc} has come back. Gone from the gate years ago over what was in the cowshed, the eldest son of the house has been a long way, to a monk on a mountain, and has come back with four small bottles in a cloth: white, blue, red, and one more. The house behind you is very quiet. The cowsheds are quiet, and there are fewer people in it than there were. {npc} stands in the road and looks at you, and you both know the end of this story.

choices.text: Open the gate, give {npc} the house back, and walk away up the hill

effects.log: You stand aside. {npc} walks past you into the empty yard with the four bottles still corked in the cloth and does not turn round. You go up the hill in your own shape, nine tails and all, in daylight. Behind you, someone begins to cry.

choices.text: Go out to the road and ask {npc} what the monk said

ok.log: "The monk said the fox would not stop," {npc} says. "That is why there are four bottles." You say that you have stopped. {npc} looks at the bottles for a long time and puts them back in the cloth. "Then I will keep these," {npc} says, "in case."

fail.log: {npc} does not wait to talk. The white bottle breaks at your feet, and the thorns come up through your coat. You get out of them, bleeding, and do not follow. Behind you {npc} walks into the empty house. (-15 health)

choices.text: Run after {npc}, as the story goes, past the thorns and the river and the fire

effects.log: The white bottle, and a thicket of thorns. The blue, and a river. The red, and a field of fire that runs to the sky. You go into it at full stretch with nine tails burning, and it burns you smaller, and smaller, down to the size of a mosquito. The summer is very long.

events.text: Years after the four bottles, {npc} keeps the house at the mouth of the valley again, with a family in it and cattle in the shed. On the shrine stone on your hill there is a bowl of rice every spring, and on top of it, always, a single cork from a small bottle.

choices.text: Eat the rice and keep the corks

effects.log: You have nine corks by the time {npc} stops coming. You keep them in the earth under the mound, in a row. They are the only gifts in all your years that were also threats, and you find you treasure them.

choices.text: Watch over the cowshed every full moon, from the hill

effects.log: Not one cow in that shed dies young for as long as {npc} lives. The family says the house is lucky now. {npc} knows exactly what kind of luck it is.

events.text: An old grey fox in a monk's robe comes up your hill on a misty morning and sits down on your grave mound without asking. Older than you, by the smell: the salt of the West Sea in its fur. "There is an island," it says, "and a pool on it, and a Dragon King's family under the pool. I have found a chant that lifts them out of the water like fish in a net, helpless. One of them a dawn, and what a dragon's child is worth to a fox's bead you can imagine. I need a second voice. Nine tails would do nicely."

choices.text: Go with it to the island

effects.log: Three days of sea fog in a fishing boat that the old fox steers without touching. The island is all rock and seabirds, and in the middle of it, a round pool as dark as an eye. Something under the water knows you have come.

choices.text: Refuse it. The old way is the old way, whatever lives it takes

effects.log: "Fastidious," says the old fox, and goes back down the hill into the fog. You sit on the mound a long time after, with the salt smell still on the grass, and wonder how many foxes it asked before you.

choices.text: Go to the shore and warn the West Sea, whatever it costs

ok.log: You stand in the surf at dusk and say it to the sea: the island, the pool, the chant. Nothing answers. But the next morning there is a single blue-green scale on the sand at your feet, as big as a rice bowl, laid there like a receipt.

fail.log: The sea does not take messages from foxes. A wave knocks you flat and drags you half a li down the beach. You go home salted and furious, and nobody in the West Sea any the wiser. (-10 health)

events.text: Dawn on the island. The old fox in its robe sits on the rock above the dragon pool and begins to chant, a dry, endless sound with no breath in it, and the black water of the pool begins to rise in a hump, and in the hump, turning helplessly like fish in a lifted net, are dragons: an old one, and a small one, and one with pearls in its whiskers. The old fox nods to you without stopping. Your turn.

choices.text: Chant with it

effects.log: Two voices, and the water goes up higher. The small dragon looks at you out of the lifted pool with eyes like wet stones. You do not stop. The bead in your mouth grows heavy and warm with something that was never yours. The old fox laughs between words.

choices.text: Sit beside it, silent, and watch

effects.log: You do not chant. You do not stop it. The water rises and falls with the old fox's voice, and the sun comes up, and the chant ends, and the pool is a pool again with one fewer under it. You are part of it, either way. You know that.

choices.text: Knock the old fox off the rock in the middle of a word

ok.log: Nine tails against a robe full of old fox. It goes down the rock into the shallows with the chant stopped in its throat, and the lifted water falls back into the pool all at once like a door slamming. The old fox swims for the boat and does not look back.

fail.log: It is older than you, and meaner. It throws you into the sea with one word, and goes on chanting while you swim. But the chant has a hole in it now, and the pool sinks back, and the dragons go down. (-15 health)

events.text: A ship has come to the island, becalmed, and gone again: its crew drew lots for which of them the sea wanted, and left one archer on the rocks with a bow and a bag of rice. You have watched the archer for three days. On the third night the archer sleeps on the shore and talks in the sleep, to someone in the sea, and says yes. Tomorrow at dawn the old fox will chant again, and you with it, on the rock in plain view of the shore.

choices.text: Stay off the rock at dawn. Let the old fox chant alone

effects.log: From the reeds you hear the chant start, alone, and the water rise, and then a sound like a branch breaking. The chant stops. Something heavy goes into the sea. By noon the archer is sitting on the shore with a single white flower held carefully against their chest, and a fair wind is coming up from nowhere.

choices.text: Go down to the shore in a human face and talk to the archer first

ok.log: The archer listens to the whole thing, the island, the chant, your share of it, and says: "Then do not be on the rock tomorrow." You are not. One arrow, at dawn. The old fox falls alone. The archer, afterward, gives you a nod across the sand, which from an archer is a great deal.

fail.log: The archer has dreamed of a fox all night and takes one look at your eyes. The arrow goes through the fur of your shoulder and into the rock. You are off the island by noon, swimming, and the old fox chants alone at the next dawn, and falls. (-15 health)

choices.text: Chant at dawn, as you have every dawn

effects.log: The water rises. The dragons turn in it. And from the shore comes a sound like a branch breaking, once, and the old fox stops in the middle of a word, and so do you. You fall off the rock as what you are: an old fox with nine tails, in the shallows, with the sun coming up.

events.text: The island again, years later, because you could not stay away. The rock above the pool has a hole in it the size of an arrowhead. The pool is quiet. On the shore a fisherman tells anyone who will listen about an archer who was left here once, and went home with a dragon's daughter carried as a flower in their breast, and two dragons escorting the ship.

choices.text: Sit by the pool and say you are sorry, to the water

effects.log: You say it once, plainly. The pool does nothing for an hour. Then a small ring spreads on it, from the middle, the way a ring spreads when something underneath has turned over in its sleep.

choices.text: Ask the fisherman for the end of the story

effects.log: The dragon's daughter became a person again when the archer got home, the fisherman says, and they had a house on the hill above the West Sea. "And the fox?" you ask. "Which fox?" says the fisherman. "There are always foxes."

events.text: The capital is the last place a fox with your history should be, which is why you came: a million faces, and nobody looks at any of them. But the fox hunters of three provinces have sent your description to the city watch, and the watch has done something unheard of and read it. There are dogs at the gates now. Yellow ones.

choices.text: Hide the tails a whole year: no lamps, no moon, no dogs

effects.log: A year in the dark. You go out only at noon, when shadows are short, and walk on the side of the street away from the shop doors. The dogs at the gates grow fat and bored.

choices.text: Keep your face and dare them

effects.log: You walk past the yellow dogs at the south gate every morning on your way to the market, and every morning they raise their hackles, and every morning the watch looks at you and decides you are only a person dogs do not like. So far.

choices.text: Leave the capital for the hills before the snow

effects.log: Out by the west gate in a carter's face, with a load of cabbages. The yellow dogs bark at the cabbages. In the hills you let your tails out for the first time in a year, and they ache like stiff legs.

events.text: A salt peddler has set up in the capital market, an old one, with an A-frame and a forked stick that is very worn at the fork. Every morning the peddler sits in the same corner and watches the crowd go by, not looking for anything. Just looking. On the third morning the stick turns, very slightly, toward you.

choices.text: Walk straight past the peddler, the way an honest person would

ok.log: You walk past. The stick does not move. Behind you, the peddler says to nobody, "Hm," in a voice like a door closing. You do not run. You will never know if you were let go.

fail.log: You walk past. The stick knocks once on the cobbles behind you, and a yellow dog three stalls away stands up and starts toward you. You turn into an alley and out of the capital's sight, and your heart does not slow down until night.

choices.text: Buy salt from the peddler, and look the stick in the eye

effects.log: "A measure of the coarse," you say. The peddler weighs it out without hurry and hands it over, and holds the stick between you a moment longer than necessary. "Use it on your doorstep," the peddler says. "Keeps things out."

choices.text: Stay out of the market until the peddler moves on

effects.log: Salt peddlers move on. They always have. You go hungry for a month buying everything from the wrong end of town, and one morning the corner is empty. You do not trust it.

events.text: Lantern night in the capital market. A lamp in a shop doorway, a paper door behind you, and you feel it before you see it: your shadow on the paper is wrong. Nine tails. A child points. Someone screams. The yellow dogs come down the street from both ends, and at the corner the salt peddler is standing up, with the stick.

choices.text: Turn over three times in the crowd and come up as somebody else

ok.log: Over, over, over, and you come up as a fat rice merchant shouting about foxes louder than anyone. The dogs run past you. The stick passes within a hand's breadth. By midnight the market is sure the fox went over the roofs.

fail.log: Over, over, and the stick catches you on the third turn, across the back. You come up as a fox in the middle of the street and run anyway, and lose them in the sewers by the river, and lie there till dawn. (-15 health)

choices.text: Stand still in the lamplight and let them look

ok.log: You stand still. The tails are there. The crowd stops, and stares, and for a long moment nobody does anything at all. Then an old woman says, "That is the herb seller from the east lane. That one set my grandson's arm." Somebody laughs. The dogs sit down. It is not safety. It is a reprieve.

fail.log: You stand still. The stick comes down on the cobbles in front of you, and the dogs come in, and you are gone over the roofs after all with a torn ear and the whole capital awake. (-15 health)

choices.text: Drop into the canal under the lantern bridge and let the water carry your scent away

effects.log: Cold black water, lanterns sliding over your head, the dogs barking at the bridge rail. You come out a mile downstream as nobody at all, and lie in the reeds till dawn. The face is gone, and the capital will tell the story for a generation, but you are alive in it. (-8 health)

choices.text: Run

effects.log: Through the lanterns, over the stalls, the whole market behind you and the dogs in front. You run, and run, out of the capital and into the hills, and the hunters of three provinces follow your tails into the end of the story.

events.text: The children of the capital have a new game. One is the fox, with a broom for nine tails, and the rest are dogs, and one, the oldest, is the salt peddler with a stick. The fox always gets away. That is the rule of the game. Nobody remembers who made it.

choices.text: Watch the game from a doorway, and teach the fox a better trick

effects.log: Turn over three times, you tell the child with the broom, and shout about foxes louder than anyone. The child does, and wins, and the game is never the same again. Long afterward it is still played that way.

choices.text: Leave the capital and its games alone for a long while

effects.log: A long while in the hills. When you come back, the game is still played, and the fox still always gets away, and nobody can tell you why.

events.text: Three villages climb your mountain now on the first and fifteenth of every month, with candles and rice and a white cloth, to the little shrine where the mountain goddess used to sit. They pray to you. They call you the Spirit of the Mountain. And every time, an old woman in a faded jacket sits on the rock outside the shrine with her hands in her sleeves, and watches them come in, and says nothing at all.

choices.text: Send the villages to the old woman on the rock

effects.log: You put a dream in the headman's head: not me, her. The next first of the month half the village bows to the old woman on the rock, puzzled. She looks at you across the clearing and nods once, the way one landlord nods to another.

choices.text: Take the prayers. They are only rice and candles

effects.log: Rice, candles, a white cloth, a hundred small wishes: rain, sons, the right husband, the wrong husband gone. You grant the easy ones. The old woman on the rock watches the candles burn down and says nothing.

choices.text: Share the shrine: half the candles on her side

effects.log: You move the candles yourself, at night, half to one side and half to the other. The villagers think it is a miracle and pray harder, to both of you. The old woman laughs, once, a dry sound like a branch in frost.

events.text: The sky over the mountain has been clear for a year and does not look like weather. It looks like attention. And you have found, sitting in the shrine with the villages' candles round you, that you can do the old trick from the oldest tale: throw a strip of paper into the air and have it come down as a blade of fire. You have done it three times, alone, at night. The third time the old woman on the rock was watching.

choices.text: Practise the fiery blades until you could fight heaven with them

effects.log: Paper, fire, paper, fire, until the clearing is ringed with scorched pines. The villagers bring more candles. The clear sky over the mountain gets clearer, in a way that makes your fur stand up.

choices.text: Give the old woman her shrine back, tonight

effects.log: You put the white cloth in her lap and walk out of the shrine. She sits in it for the first time in years, and the candles straighten. The sky over the mountain clouds over in the morning, ordinarily, and rains, and it is the most beautiful rain you have ever seen.

choices.text: Ask the old woman what she wants

effects.log: "My shrine," she says. "My mountain. My villages, who are fools, but mine." Then, after a long time: "And for you to be what you are, somewhere else." It is the most honest thing anyone has said to you in a century.

events.text: Heaven comes at noon. First the wind, which takes the shrine roof off in one piece and sets it down in the next valley. Then the rain, which is not rain but a wall. Then the lightning, which stands over the mountain and does not strike yet, and waits. Three great shapes in the weather, and the old woman on the rock, quite dry, with her hands in her sleeves.

choices.text: Kneel in the rain, and give the old woman her mountain

effects.log: You put your forehead in the mud in front of the rock. The wind stops. The rain stops. The lightning stands a long time over you, thinking, and then goes back into the sky. The old woman gets up, walks past you into her shrine, and from the doorway says: "Go home, fox."

choices.text: Run from the mountain with the storm on your tails

ok.log: Down the ridge, across three valleys, through a river. The wind follows you to the second valley and the rain to the river, and the lightning watches you go from the top of the mountain and lets you. The villages will pray to the old woman now. (-10 health)

fail.log: The lightning lets you get as far as the river, and then reminds you. You crawl out on the far bank with your tails smoking. The villages will pray to the old woman now. You will not come back. (-15 health)

choices.text: Throw the papers into the air and fight them with fire

effects.log: Blades of fire against wind, rain and lightning. You are magnificent for nearly a minute. Then the lightning strikes, and the roof of the world comes down on the shrine, and when the rain stops the villages find only a great fox in the ash, and the old woman goes home to her shrine.

events.text: The old woman's shrine has a new roof, and the three villages climb to it twice a month, and pray to her as if they had never stopped. Every spring, on your grave mound, someone leaves a rice cake on a leaf and a single scorched strip of paper, folded very small.

choices.text: Take the rice cake, and leave the paper

effects.log: You eat the cake. The paper you leave on the mound in the rain until it is pulp. It is a message, and you have read it: I remember. So do you.

choices.text: Go up and bow to the old woman, once

effects.log: She is sitting on the rock outside her own shrine, as if she liked it better there. You bow. She does not bow back. But she moves over on the rock, a little, and you sit beside her and watch the villages come up the path.

events.text: The new governor of the province is cold. He has always been cold, his steward tells the market, and nothing warms his neck in winter, and a physician has told him that only one thing will: a collar of white fox, from a fox that has lived a thousand years. The bounty is three hundred sacks of rice. The hunters of three counties have stopped arguing with each other.

choices.text: Find out everything about the governor, in a servant's face

effects.log: A month in the governor's kitchen. He is cold because he does not eat. He does not eat because he is afraid of poison. He is afraid of poison because he poisoned the last governor. Everything in a house like that is a fox's business.

choices.text: Go deep into the hills until the governor's term is up

effects.log: Governors serve three years. You can wait three years in a cave. You can wait thirty. In the cave you hear the horns of the hunt every morning, further away each winter.

choices.text: Lead the first hunters into the marsh with foxfire

ok.log: Three nights, a marsh, a dozen torches going round and round the same reed bed. On the fourth morning the hunters walk out muddy to the waist and swear off white foxes. The governor hires more.

fail.log: One of them carries a dog that does not follow lights. It follows you. You lose it in a river at dawn and lie in the reeds shivering, a white fox in brown water. (-10 health)

events.text: A trap in the snow on the hill road, and the bait is a smell. Not meat. A fox's smell, one you knew in the earth under the mound a thousand years ago, rubbed on a stake from an old pelt that someone has kept all this time in a chest. The hunters know what a fox will come to.

choices.text: Go to it anyway, carefully, to see whose it was

ok.log: You get to the stake without touching the snare, and put your nose to it, and know the smell. A littermate, from the first earth. You take the scrap of old fur off the stake in your teeth and carry it away and bury it under your mound, where it should have been all along.

fail.log: The snare takes your foreleg. You are out of it in a breath, at the cost of skin and fur, and the scrap of old pelt comes with you in your teeth. The hunters find blood, white hair, and nothing else. (-15 health)

choices.text: Leave it. The dead are not bait, and you are not a fool

effects.log: You go round the long way. It is the wise thing. All winter the smell of that stake is on the wind, and you dream of the earth under the mound every night, and wake with your tails over your nose.

choices.text: Spring the trap from a distance and let the hunters find it empty

effects.log: A stone, well aimed. The snare snaps on nothing. The hunters find it at dawn, empty and sprung, with the stake knocked flat and white fox hair on it, laid there neatly, on purpose. They go home and tell the governor he is being laughed at.

events.text: The governor's own hunt in the first snow: a hundred men, forty dogs, falcons, drums. They have found your hill, and they have done the one thing you did not think of. They are burning the village at the foot of it, one house at a time, the houses whose people put rice cakes on your grave mound, and the drums are saying: come out.

choices.text: Fight them for the village, with everything you have

ok.log: Foxfire on every roof that is not burning, a fan of nine tails across the road, dogs that will not go near you. The hunt breaks at dusk and runs. The village stands, mostly. The governor writes to the capital for soldiers. (-15 health)

fail.log: Too many men, too many dogs. You get the village's children out of the fire and up the hill, and that is all. The hunt goes home with three white hairs and a story. (-15 health)

choices.text: Lead the whole hunt away over three mountains

ok.log: A white flash on the far ridge, and the drums turn after it. You lead them over one mountain, two, three. On the fourth day the hunt is lost in a gorge and the governor is very cold indeed. The village puts out its fires.

fail.log: They split: half after you, half staying to burn. You come back too late for two houses. The governor has nearly enough white hairs for a cuff. (-15 health)

choices.text: Go down in a steward's face and sell the governor a better hunt three valleys away

effects.log: A steward with a map, very respectful, very sure: the white fox dens in the next prefecture, everyone knows it. The governor believes a map from a stranger over his own drums, as governors do. The burning stops. The hunt moves on to a valley where there is no fox at all, and you are ashamed of how easy it was.

choices.text: Come out, and let them take you, if the burning stops

effects.log: You walk down the hill in the snow in plain sight, nine tails, white as the snow, and the drums stop, and the burning stops. The governor wears a white collar all that winter. In later lives it is a priceless, uneasy treasure, and the village at the foot of the hill never forgets why it still stands.

events.text: The governor who wanted a white fox collar has been recalled to the capital in disgrace: something about a poisoned predecessor and a letter that turned up in the wrong hands. The new governor is warm-necked and lazy and has taken the bounty boards down. On the step of your earth, one morning, there is a small bundle of white rabbit fur, tied with string, from the village.

choices.text: Line the earth with it, and sleep warm all winter

effects.log: Rabbit, not fox. A joke and a gift at once, from people who have watched you for a long time. You sleep the whole winter on it with your nose under your tails, and dream of nothing at all.

choices.text: Leave it at the door of the poorest house in the village

effects.log: It goes round the village all winter, from neck to neck, and comes back to your step in spring, thinner, with a second string tied round it. Nobody says a word about it, ever.

events.text: A young monk has been sitting under your pine all summer, very still, doing the hard kind of meditation that has no words in it. And on the next ridge an older monk has built a hermitage and does the noisy kind: drums, bells, spells shouted at the sky until the whole mountain shakes and your earth sheds soil on your nose. The young one, {npc}, cannot hear a thought. Neither, now, can the mountain.
events.arc: The Black Fox Under the Pine

choices.text: Warn the drummer three times, bring the hillside down on the empty hermitage, and send {npc} west to study

mem.note: sent me west, and swore to keep me

effects.log: Three warnings, three sneers. Then a night of lightning and a landslide on an empty hermitage; the drummer, alive and furious, leaves the mountain. In the quiet you speak to {npc} in a voice out of the pine: go west, study, come back. {npc} promises. You promise back: to keep {npc} in this life and the lives after. Mountains like that kind of promise.

choices.text: Leave the drummer, and only send {npc} west with the promise

mem.note: swore from the pine to keep me

effects.log: "Go where it is quiet enough to learn," you say from the pine. "Come back when you know something. I will keep you, in this life and the next." {npc} bows to the tree for a very long time and goes west in the morning. Eleven years. You count them.

choices.text: Let them both be. Monks are not a fox's business

effects.log: The drums go on, and the young monk goes home in the autumn with nothing learned. The mountain grumbles in its sleep. It wanted something of you, and you did not give it.

events.text: A charcoal-burner's child of nine comes up the mountain alone in the snow, past every path the family uses, straight to your pine, and sits down under it as if it were a hearth. {npc} has a fever and a cough and no idea why they came. You know why. You made a promise to someone who sat in exactly that place, in exactly that way, a lifetime ago.
events.arc: The Black Fox Under the Pine

choices.text: Lend the bead for a night, and carry {npc} home asleep before dawn

mem.note: woke at home with the fever gone and pine needles in my hair

effects.log: One night of the bead on a breath, and the fever goes out like a coal in snow. You carry {npc} down the mountain in your mouth like a kit, and leave them on the charcoal-burner's step with pine needles in their hair. Once.

choices.text: Keep {npc} warm under your tails till the fever breaks on its own

effects.log: Three days and nights in the snow with a feverish child curled in nine tails. On the fourth morning {npc} wakes, looks up at you without fear, and says: "I knew it was here." Once. (-6 health)

events.text: Your coat is darkening. It began at the tail-tips, the way the white did, and goes inward a little every winter: not grey, not brown, but black, black as lacquer on a good table, with the white left only at the muzzle. The mountain is taking you as its spirit, a hair at a time. {npc}, grown now and a monk like the one before, has climbed to the pine to ask one thing: "Show me what you really are. Once. Then I will never ask again."
events.arc: The Black Fox Under the Pine

choices.text: Show {npc}: lift one arm of the mountain into the sky

effects.log: Not a fox at all, for one breath: an arm of cloud and pine and stone reaching up from the mountain into the sky, so long it touches the clouds. Then a black fox under a pine. {npc} sits down very hard in the snow. By spring the whole province calls it Long Arm Mountain, and nobody knows why.

choices.text: Show {npc} only an old black fox, which is also true

effects.log: You let the face and the shadow and the mountain go, and there is just you, black-coated, white-muzzled, very old. {npc} looks for a long time. "That is enough," {npc} says. "That is more than enough."

choices.text: Refuse kindly. A mountain is not something to look at

effects.log: {npc} laughs and bows and does not ask again, as promised. But on the way down the path you see {npc} stop and look back up at the mountain with an expression you know: someone who has decided to find out anyway, in some other life.

events.text: The third life. A young monk at the small temple at the foot of the mountain, who has never climbed it, dreams every night of a pine and a black fox and a promise, and does not understand the dream. And this spring the snow on the north face has gone soft all at once, and is hanging over the temple roof like a held breath.
events.arc: The Black Fox Under the Pine

choices.text: Hold the snow on the mountain with your whole weight until {npc} is out

ok.log: A whole night lying across the north face with nine black tails dug into the snow, holding. At dawn {npc} wakes from the dream, for once, and walks out of the temple gate to see the sunrise, and the snow comes down behind into an empty yard. Twice.

fail.log: You cannot hold it. The snow goes, and you go with it, and at the bottom you dig with both forepaws in the dark until you find {npc} under the temple beam, alive, and drag them out by the sleeve. Twice. It nearly cost the mountain its spirit. (-15 health)

choices.text: Go down in a woodcutter's face and get the whole temple out on some excuse

ok.log: A woodcutter who says a bear is in the kitchen, very convincingly. Every monk in the temple is in the yard with a stick when the snow comes down on the empty kitchen. {npc} looks at the woodcutter afterwards for a long, puzzled moment, as if remembering a dream.

fail.log: The monks do not believe a woodcutter about bears. You end up carrying {npc} out of the gate over your shoulder, shouting, a moment before the snow, and the face slips, and the whole temple sees black fur. They will talk about it for a century. (-15 health)

events.text: Thirteen hundred years and more, and you are tired the way a mountain is tired: all through, without hurry. You lie down under the pine one autumn and find you do not want to get up. Down the slope a monk is climbing toward you, old now, slow, with a stick: {npc}, in the last of the three lives, coming up the mountain for the first time, following a dream to the end.
events.arc: The Black Fox Under the Pine

choices.text: Not yet. Get up, and meet {npc} halfway, and keep the mountain a while longer

effects.log: You get up, all of your years, and walk down to meet {npc} on the path, and the two of you sit on a rock and watch the valley go dark. "There is still a little more," you say. "Then a little more," says {npc}. The mountain agrees.

choices.text: Wait for {npc} under the pine, and let the promise finish

effects.log: {npc} reaches the pine at sunset and kneels, and puts a hand on your black coat, and knows everything at once. "Three times," {npc} says. You close your eyes. The monk names the mountain after the promise, and the shrine at the top has a black fox on it to this day.

events.text: A monk came back from the west with years of learning, a long time ago, and went down the mountain to teach, and grew old teaching, and died. You were not there. Mountains are not allowed at funerals. Now the monk's disciples have carried a small stone up to your pine and set it at the roots, and on it is carved one word: kept.
events.arc: The Black Fox Under the Pine

choices.text: Lie with your chin on the stone for a season

effects.log: One word. You lie with it all winter and the snow covers you both. Mountains do not weep, but in the spring there is a new spring on the slope below the pine, very cold and very clear, and the temple takes its water from it.

choices.text: Go down and walk among the disciples, in a passing monk's face

effects.log: A passing monk in a worn robe who knows every one of the teacher's sayings, including two nobody wrote down. The disciples argue about it for years. You are, you decide, allowed this much of a funeral.

events.text: Every dusk a student walks the hill road past your mound to the village school, late, books in a cloth under one arm, reciting under their breath and getting it wrong. {npc} is sixteen and slow at the classics and the whole family's hope for the county examination. It is the oldest road in the oldest story. You have walked beside a great many students on it. This time you would like the story to end differently.
events.arc: The One Who Looked at the Earth

choices.text: Walk beside {npc} at dusk in a borrowed face, at arm's length, and correct the recitation

effects.log: "Heaven is dark, earth is yellow," you say. "Not the other way round." {npc} goes red, then laughs, then asks who you are. A traveller, you say. Every evening after that there is a traveller on the hill road, never closer than an arm's length, who knows every word of every book.

choices.text: Leave a lit lantern on the worst bend of the road every dusk

effects.log: Every evening a paper lantern on a stake at the bend by the grave mounds, lit. {npc} never finds out who. The village says it is the lucky fox of the hill. For once, the village is exactly right.

choices.text: Only watch, this time, from the long grass

effects.log: You watch {npc} go up the road and down it, all autumn, getting the recitation wrong. It is a kind of company. It is not the kind the story wants.

events.text: The schoolmaster has noticed. An old one, nearly blind, who has taught on this hill for forty years and heard every story. Today, you hear through the floor, the lesson stopped for an hour while the schoolmaster told {npc} the old one: a stranger on the hill road, a bead that passes on a breath, a student who grows pale. "And if it ever happens to you," the schoolmaster said, "swallow it, and look at the sky."
events.arc: The One Who Looked at the Earth

choices.text: Keep walking with {npc}. You have never taken a breath from this one

effects.log: {npc} walks beside you that evening a little further away than usual, and then, at the bend, a little closer. "You have never once made me pale," {npc} says. "I checked." You laugh out loud on the hill road for the first time in a century.

choices.text: Go to the schoolmaster that night and pour the tea yourself

effects.log: The schoolmaster does not turn round. "Sit," the old voice says. "I thought you would come. Is it the bead you want, or the student?" Neither, you say. "Then you are the strangest fox in the old book," says the schoolmaster, "and I should like to know how it ends."

events.text: The last evening before {npc} leaves for the county examination. On the hill road, at the bend by the mounds, you stop, and {npc} stops, an arm's length away. You know what you are going to do. You have known for a year. You take the bead out of your mouth and hold it in your open palm, a small moon, and the student goes very still.
events.arc: The One Who Looked at the Earth

choices.text: Lend it, for one night only, and take it back at dawn

effects.log: One night of the bead's understanding on a breath, and at dawn it comes back, and {npc} walks to the county town with the classics clear as water. Pass, third in the province. {npc} never knows why, and stops at your mound on the way home, and bows to it, just in case.

choices.text: Put it back in your mouth and wish {npc} luck

effects.log: You close your hand. "Luck," you say, and mean it. {npc} goes down to the county town with the classics as muddled as ever, and fails, and comes home, and tries again, and passes at thirty. Some roads are walked alone. That is not the worst ending.

choices.text: Give it, and say: "Swallow it, and look at the sky"

effects.log: {npc} swallows it, and turns to run as the story says, and trips on a root, and falls flat, and looks at the earth. Every vein of qi in the hill, every good grave, every spring under every field. For years the great geomancer of three provinces has a fox's voice in one ear. You end with one tail and no power, and do not mind at all.

events.text: {npc}, middle-aged now, in an official's robe, climbs the hill road with a geomancer's compass on a cord and stops at your mound. "They want to put the magistrate's father on this hill," {npc} says to the grass. "I told them the qi here runs wrong. It does not. I lied to a magistrate for a fox. I would like to know whether it was worth it."
events.arc: The One Who Looked at the Earth

choices.text: Answer from the grass: "It was. The fox is grateful"

mem.note: thanked me on the hill road

effects.log: {npc} sits down on the mound, laughs, and takes out a flask and two cups, and pours one onto the grass. You have not been given a drink by a friend in a hundred years. You drink it.

choices.text: Show {npc} where the qi really runs, under the whole hill

effects.log: All afternoon, a fox walking ahead and a geomancer following with a compass. By dusk {npc} has three pages of notes and a face like a child at a festival. The family has never chosen a bad site since.

events.text: A famine winter. On a grave mound at the edge of the pines, in the snow, someone has left a baby in a basket with a bowl of millet and a strip of white cloth: the way people leave a child they cannot feed for the spirits to take. The baby is alive and furious about it. {npc} has a voice like a little bell.

choices.text: Raise {npc} yourself, in the face of an herb-seller at the edge of the village

mem.note: raised me from a basket in the snow

effects.log: An herb-seller at the edge of the village takes in a foundling that winter, and the village thinks it very kind and a little odd. Twenty years, you tell yourself. You can keep a face for years. {npc} grabs your finger and will not let go.

choices.text: Carry the basket to the temple gate before dawn

effects.log: You leave it on the step of the temple at the foot of the mountain, and ring the bell with your tail, and go. The monks raise the child. Years later a novice comes up the mountain every spring with a bowl of millet, and leaves it on that mound, and does not know why.

choices.text: Leave the basket at the headman's door with a lantern lit beside it

effects.log: The headman opens the door at dawn to a lantern nobody lit and a baby nobody will claim. The headman's household keeps it. You watch the child grow up from the hill, and it is a perfectly ordinary, happy child, which is a very great deal.

events.text: {npc} is a child still, and quicker than any child in the valley: can catch a hare in a field barehanded, can find the way home in the dark without a light, and never, ever gets lost on the hill. The village children have a name for it, and shout it in the lanes: fox-born. {npc} comes home and asks you what it means.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the truth, all of it, quietly, by the hearth

ok.log: {npc} listens to the whole of it with eyes getting rounder and rounder, and at the end asks only, "Can I see the tails?" You show one. {npc} touches it, very carefully, and says, "I knew it," and goes to bed, and keeps the secret for the rest of a long life.

fail.log: {npc} does not believe a word, then believes all of it at once and cries, and in the morning tells the whole lane that the herb-seller is a fox. Nobody believes it. Children say such things. You hide the tails very carefully for a year.

choices.text: Tell {npc} it means quick, and clever, and lucky

effects.log: "Like a fox," you say, "the best kind." {npc} goes out the next day and wears the name like a badge, and by the end of the summer the children have stopped shouting it, because it is no fun when the fox-born child shouts it back.

choices.text: Take {npc} up the hill at night and show the way the fox goes

effects.log: Every path, every earth, every stream that breaks a trail. {npc} learns the hill in a season the way you learned it in a century. Later, much later, it will save an army.

events.text: {npc} is grown, and goes to the army in a bad year, and comes home in a good one as a captain, and then a general. The soldiers say the general can catch a tiger with bare hands and smell an ambush through a wall. The villages say what they always said, louder: fox-born. {npc} stops at your door on the way to the capital, in armour, and does not quite know how to say goodbye to the one who raised them.

choices.text: Say goodbye the way you did when {npc} was small: a hand on the head

effects.log: {npc} has to bend down for it now, armour creaking. Neither of you says anything. The general rides to the capital with the whole village watching, and does not look back, and you know exactly why.

choices.text: Give {npc} one red-brown hair to carry, for luck

effects.log: {npc} puts it in the lining of the helmet. Later the army will say the general's luck is uncanny. The army will be right, and never know why.

events.text: The general they call fox-born comes home on leave, grown and famous, and climbs your hill alone. {npc} was the child you raised in a borrowed face, years ago, and has never once said what they knew. Today, at the top of the hill, {npc} sits down on your mound and says to the grass: "I know. I always knew. Thank you."

choices.text: Come out of the grass and sit beside {npc}

effects.log: A general and a nine-tailed fox on a grave mound, watching the paddies go gold. {npc} talks about the army and the capital and a tiger cub in a ditch. You listen. It is the first time either of you has been anything but careful in years.

choices.text: Stay in the grass. Let it be said, and not answered

effects.log: The general waits a long time, and then nods, as if an answer had come, and goes down the hill. On the mound there is a rice cake on a clean leaf.

events.text: The governor has ordered a great fox hunt in three provinces, and given it to the best hunter in the army: {npc}, the general they call fox-born. The hunt goes through every hill in three provinces, with dogs and drums and falcons, and catches a great many foxes, and goes round one hill, every time, as if the hill were not there.

choices.text: Lie low on your hill and let {npc} keep the secret

effects.log: The drums go round your hill like a river round a rock. On the last day of the hunt a single arrow lands in the grass on your mound with no head on it. A message. You keep it in the earth with the other things worth keeping.

choices.text: Go to {npc}'s tent at night and ask that the other foxes be spared

ok.log: The general listens with a lamp between you and at the end says: "I will lose them in the mountains. All of them." The hunt comes back with nothing and the governor shouts. {npc} takes the shouting very calmly.

fail.log: "I cannot," the general says. "Not all of them. Some of them are eating children's chickens and worse. But not on your hill, and not the old ones." It is something. It is not everything.

choices.text: Leave the hill for the length of the hunt, so {npc} does not have to lie

effects.log: You go over the mountains for a season. When you come back your hill is untouched and there is a note pinned to the pine with a general's seal: you did not have to go. You did, though.

events.text: {npc} is old, and has come home to the house in the valley for the last time, and the general's banner hangs at the gate. You can see it from the slope above the house, where you lie in the autumn grass every evening now. You are tired, too, in the way that has no hurry in it.

choices.text: Go down to the gate one last time in the old herb-seller's face

effects.npcPass: old age, at the gate under the banner, holding an old herb-seller's hand
effects.log: {npc} knows the face at once, and laughs, and says, "You have not aged a day," which is the oldest joke between you. You sit at the gate until dark. {npc} dies that winter. You go on, a long way, and it is a little lonelier.

choices.text: Lie down on the slope above the house, and stay

effects.log: The general sits at the gate every evening and looks up at the slope, and you look down. In the winter they find an old fox on the hillside above the general's house, curled up with its tails over its nose, and the general has it buried on that slope with a soldier's rites, and tells nobody why.

events.text: The wine-house at the crossroads has had the same keeper for longer than any traveller knows, in one face after another: a widow, a retired soldier, a grumpy old pedlar, a young cook from the south. Tonight a grandmother stops for makgeolli and says, "My grandmother stopped here. She said the keeper had kind eyes, like yours."
events.arc: The Five-Hundredth Year at the Crossroads

choices.text: Pour the grandmother a second bowl, on the house

effects.log: "The same kind of eyes," the grandmother says again, peering at you over the bowl. You agree that it is a family trait. It is, in a way. Every keeper of this house has had them.

choices.text: Ask what else the old grandmother said

effects.log: "That nobody who stopped here ever got lost on the way home," the grandmother says. "Not once. She said the lanterns followed you." They do. You light them yourself.

events.text: The wine-house at the crossroads has stood empty three years, since the last keeper died, and the travellers go past it in the rain with their heads down. The roof leaks.
