The jars are cracked. The lantern hooks under the eaves are rusty and bare. You have been looking at it from the hill all summer, the way you look at a face you might wear.
events.arc: The Five-Hundredth Year at the Crossroads

choices.text: Take it: a borrowed face, a new roof, the lanterns lit

effects.log: A new keeper at the crossroads, with a cracked jar mended and the lanterns lit by the first frost. {npc}, a carter who has passed that way every month for twenty years, is the first through the door, and stands dripping on the step and says, "Thank heaven. Somebody."

choices.text: Mend the roof one night and leave it for someone else

effects.log: In the morning the wine-house has a sound roof and nobody can say who did it. By spring a widow from the next valley has taken it, and lit the lanterns, and you go past it at dusk and are glad.

events.text: A traveller every night at the crossroads, and all of them lost in some way: a bride's cousin who took the wrong road to the wedding, a soldier walking home from a war nobody won, a child sent for medicine who forgot which village. You have kept a rule at this house for longer than anyone knows. Everyone who stops here gets home.
events.arc: The Five-Hundredth Year at the Crossroads

choices.text: Walk the soldier home yourself, ahead, with a light on your tail

effects.log: Three days, two mountains, a light always just ahead on the path. At the soldier's own gate the light goes out. The soldier's family hears the story and does not believe it, and leaves a jar of their best at the crossroads every New Year.

choices.text: Send the child back with the right medicine and a lantern that never goes out

effects.log: Your own medicine, better than the physician's, and a paper lantern lit with a little bead-light. The child gets home by dawn. The lantern burns in that family's kitchen for years.

choices.text: Sit up all night with the bride's cousin, and tell them which road

effects.log: "The east road," you say, "and run." They get to the wedding in time to hold the gourd ladle, and they tell the story so often that the crossroads becomes a place people stop on purpose, for luck.

events.text: Centuries at the crossroads, near enough. You count it one evening with a brush on the back of the tally board in the kitchen: faces, roads, travellers, rules. The lanterns are lit. A carter is asleep on the platform. Somewhere up the hill road, someone is lost and walking toward the light.
events.arc: The Five-Hundredth Year at the Crossroads

choices.text: Not yet the end. Keep it, and keep wanting more

effects.log: You put the brush down, light another lantern, and pour for the next lost one through the door. The mountain, the moon, the human name: they can wait one more traveller. They always can.

choices.text: Keep the wine-house for as long as there are roads

effects.log: You never become human and never become a god. You keep the wine-house at the crossroads in one face after another, and every traveller who stops there gets home. It is a smaller thing than heaven. You are not sure it is a lesser one.

events.text: The kingdom is failing, and the signs know it before the ministers do. The wells in the capital have run red for a month. A great fish has come up dead on the river below the walls. The old zelkova in the palace garden makes a sound at night like someone crying. In the market, toads by the thousand have climbed into the trees, and people run from them, and are trampled. You walk through all of it in a face that suits the day, and smell the end of something.
events.arc: The Last Spring of a Kingdom

choices.text: Tell the king, in your court face, that the signs mean mend your rule

ok.log: The king hears you out, and for a season the taxes are lighter and the old ministers back from exile. It is not enough. You knew it would not be. But a season is a season, and three provinces eat through it.

fail.log: The king laughs and says the signs mean the enemy will fall. The court laughs with him. A minister at the back does not laugh, and watches your shadow on the paper door.

choices.text: Watch, and remember. Kingdoms end

effects.log: You have seen several kingdoms end, and they all ended like this: signs that everyone sees and nobody reads. You read them. You write nothing down. A fox's memory is enough.

choices.text: Go to the weeping tree at night and ask it what it knows

effects.log: The zelkova is six hundred years old and does not like foxes. But it tells you, in the end, what it has heard in the roots: horses from the east, and ships from the west, before the summer is out.

events.text: Labourers digging a new ditch in the palace grounds have turned up a turtle, alive, with writing on its back. The court gathers. The writing says: this kingdom is the full moon; the other is the new moon. The king's shaman reads it truly, aloud: the full moon can only wane. The king has the shaman taken out and killed before the turtle is back in the ditch. Then a younger man reads it again, the other way, and is made a minister.
events.arc: The Last Spring of a Kingdom

choices.text: Go to the shaman's family that night, and keep them

effects.log: A widow and two children in a back lane, already packing. You get them out of the capital by the west gate before dawn in a carter's face, and settle them in a village where nobody has heard of turtles. They light a candle for the shaman every year, and one for the carter.

choices.text: Speak for the dead shaman in court, in your face, and say the truth again

effects.log: The court goes silent. The new minister goes white. The king looks at you for a long time and decides, for reasons of his own, to laugh. You are not killed. Your shadow on the paper door is watched very carefully from now on.

choices.text: Say nothing. A fox who reads omens aloud ends on a desk

effects.log: You keep your face still while the shaman is taken out. The vixen who bore you would say it was wise. It does not feel like wisdom. It feels like the end of spring.

events.text: Spring, the last one. The plum is out in the palace and the enemy is a month away. This morning foxes have come into the palace from the hills, a whole troop of them, red and grey, padding down the corridors past the guards as if they had been invited. Nobody stops them. Nobody can. In the hall of the chief minister the doors are open, and the great lacquered desk is empty, and waiting.
events.arc: The Last Spring of a Kingdom

choices.text: Lead the foxes out of the palace before anyone writes them down

ok.log: You go down the corridors in your court face shouting about vermin, and the foxes, who know an elder when they hear one, follow you out through the kitchen gate. The court writes down only that the palace had foxes. The kingdom falls anyway, a little less certain of why.

fail.log: Half the troop follows you out. The other half goes on into the minister's hall, and one young grey fox, very pleased with itself, jumps onto the desk. The histories write it down. It is not you. It is not entirely not you.

choices.text: Leave the capital tonight, and let the spring do what springs do

effects.log: You go out of the west gate in a carter's face with plum blossom on the cart. Behind you the foxes sit in the corridors, and the kingdom falls in the summer, and somebody else's fox sits on the desk in the histories.

choices.text: Go in as yourself, and sit on the chief minister's desk in plain sight

effects.log: You walk in past the courtiers and jump up onto the desk among the scrolls and sit there with your tails round your feet, and look at them. Nobody moves. The kingdom falls in the summer, and the histories write you down as its last sign, and read you that way still.

events.text: A black serpent as thick as a temple rope is coiled at the mouth of your earth one morning, and it speaks with two voices, because the other voice is very far away in the north, inside a shell. "The council of the four directions," says the serpent. "Has never heard a fox," says the far voice. "It will hear one," they finish together. "Bring your ledger. Bring your faces."
events.arc: The Four Guardians Look at a Fox

choices.text: Bow to the north

effects.log: The serpent approves. The far voice says it has seen better bows, from a tiger, once. They argue about which tiger for the rest of the morning, and you understand that this is how the north does everything.

choices.text: Ask why the council would hear a fox at all

effects.log: "Because you asked to climb," says the serpent. "And everything that climbs," says the far voice, "passes the four walls of the sky." "Even a fox," says the serpent, as if this were the strangest sentence it had ever been part of.

choices.text: Ask which face they would like you to bring

effects.log: There is a long silence in two places. "Your own," says the serpent at last. "If you can find it," says the far voice, and the serpent laughs, a dry sound like ice cracking on a river.

events.text: The Azure Dragon comes to the council from the east, and the terrace goes blue-green with its storm, and it does not look at you. It lays down a list in claw marks on a slab of slate: every pool, every egg and every dragon's child that ever suffered at a fox's hand, and your name against the ones that are yours. "I speak against it," the east says. "Foxes have been the enemies of dragons since the first pool. Let it say why this one is different."
events.arc: The Four Guardians Look at a Fox

choices.text: Answer for every line on the slate, the true ones too

effects.log: It takes a long time. Some lines you defend. Most you cannot. At the end the dragon takes back its slate and looks at it a while. "Fewer excuses than I expected," it says. That, from the east, is a beginning.

choices.text: Say only: "It is not different. It is sorry"

ok.log: The storm on the east of the terrace goes still. "Sorry," the dragon repeats, as if testing a coin with its teeth. "Foxes do not say that." It does not withdraw a word. But it does not add one, either, and the north writes that down.

fail.log: "Foxes say many things," the east says, and the storm stays. The north writes it all down on the inside of its shell. The climb, you understand, will be steeper for this.

events.text: The Azure Dragon comes to the council from the east, and lies down on the terrace near you, closer than any dragon has ever lain to a fox. "I speak for it," the east says. "Foxes are the enemies of dragons since the first pool. This one has done dragons good turns, some that I know of and some I only suspect. I do not like foxes. I will speak for this one as long as you like."
events.arc: The Four Guardians Look at a Fox

choices.text: Thank the east, in front of everyone

effects.log: "Do not," says the dragon, embarrassed, and looks away east for a long time. The Black Tortoise writes something on its shell. Somewhere in the south, a bird laughs.

choices.text: Tell the council the times you were tempted, and nearly did not

effects.log: There are more than the dragon knew. It listens to all of them with its whiskers flat, and at the end says, "Nearly is the whole of it," and on the way out walks beside you for a while.

events.text: The Azure Dragon comes to the council from the east and looks at you for a long time, as a farmer looks at a field that has never been planted. "I do not know this fox," it says. "Foxes have been the enemies of dragons since the first pool, and this one has never once come near mine. I have nothing to say for it and nothing against it. Let the others speak."
events.arc: The Four Guardians Look at a Fox

choices.text: Say that you kept away from dragons out of fear, and say it plainly

effects.log: "Fear," says the dragon. "That is honest." It turns its head to the north. "Write down that it was honest." The north writes. It is not much. On this terrace it is not nothing.

choices.text: Promise the east a debt: one good turn to a dragon, before you climb

effects.log: "Done," says the dragon, surprised into it. You will spend a whole spring clearing a silted spring in the eastern hills for a young dragon who never knows who did it. The east knows.

events.text: The White Tiger comes to the council from the west, with autumn in its coat, and sits down across the terrace and looks at you with yellow eyes that remember something. "A sunshower," it says. "A long time ago. A stream between two hills, and a small red fox on the far bank that did not run. I was young. So were you." It yawns, which shows every tooth it has. "That was a greeting," it tells the council. "I have been waiting a thousand years to see what the fox would do with it."
events.arc: The Four Guardians Look at a Fox

choices.text: Yawn back, across the terrace

effects.log: You show every tooth you have. The Vermilion Bird laughs so hard it sets fire to a corner of the north's record, and the serpent has to put it out. The White Tiger looks, for a moment, extremely pleased.

choices.text: Tell the White Tiger what you did with it: a thousand years, told honestly

effects.log: The masks, the borrowed years, the hunters, the dogs. The tiger listens to all of it the way the west listens: weighing. "Hm," it says at the end. "The beam came out nearer level than I thought."

events.text: The White Tiger comes to the council from the west, with autumn in its coat, and sniffs the air on your side of the terrace with great suspicion. "Foxes," it says, "stole from my grandmother. The soft things other tigers left her. Every fox on the mountain. Which of them were you?"
events.arc: The Four Guardians Look at a Fox

choices.text: "None. But I would have, at that age"

effects.log: The tiger stares. Then makes a sound in its chest like a rockfall, which is a tiger laughing. "So would I," it says. "She was very slow." The north writes something down and the serpent asks it to cross it out.

choices.text: "I will pay her debt, whoever owed it"

effects.log: "She is dead," says the tiger. "A long time." Then, after a while: "There is a shrine for her on the saddle of the west ridge. Leave a hare there once a year." You do, for a century. The west notices.

events.text: The Vermilion Bird comes up from the south in a column of heat, every feather a flame, and does not read the Breath ledger. It sings it. Every breath you ever borrowed, by name and village and the colour of the face in the morning, and after each one, if it was given back, a second, softer note. The council listens without moving. You listen to the whole of it, and so do the stars.
events.arc: The Four Guardians Look at a Fox

choices.text: Name each one with the bird, the given-back and the still-owed

effects.log: You know every name. The bird sings each a little softer than the last, and at the end bows to you, unexpectedly. "You know them," it says. "The ones who borrow usually forget."

choices.text: Ask for a century to give back the last of them before you climb

effects.log: The council grants it. The tortoise says a century is short. The serpent says for a fox it is long. The bird says nothing, and burns a little warmer, and waits.

choices.text: Ask the bird to sing the short song: you never borrowed one

effects.log: The bird looks at you for a long time out of an eye like a coal. Then it sings the clean ninth tail and the thousand days, and the silence where the ledger would be. It is a much shorter song, and a stranger one, and the north writes it on its shell twice.

choices.text: Listen in silence, and let the bird finish

effects.log: The song goes on a long while. When it ends the whole terrace is quiet, and the bird bows its flaming head to you, once, and burns on.

events.text: The Yellow Dragon of the centre, of earth and of the late summer between all seasons, has said nothing through the whole hearing. Now it lifts its head and weighs you, the way a farmer weighs a sack of grain in two hands. "A fox," it says. "A thing of masks. Every one of the four walls of the sky is what it is, all the way through. Why should a fox, which is never what it seems, walk on the moon road?"
events.arc: The Four Guardians Look at a Fox

choices.text: "Because I was always what I seemed to the people I was kind to"

ok.log: The Yellow Dragon considers it for a whole night. "The face was false," it says in the morning. "The kindness was not. Hm." It looks at the others. Nobody disagrees, which on that terrace is a verdict. The north writes: heard.

fail.log: The centre does not argue. It only goes on looking at you, with the patience of farmland, until you look away. But the north writes: heard. That is all the hearing ever promised.

choices.text: "I do not know. I have been finding out for a very long time"

effects.log: "Good," says the Yellow Dragon. "The ones who know already are the ones who fall off the road." The Vermilion Bird sings one note. Even the serpent nods. The north writes: heard.

choices.text: Show the centre your own face, for once: an old fox, nothing else

effects.log: You let every face go, every shadow, every trick of the light, and sit on the terrace as what you are. The Yellow Dragon looks at you a long while. "There," it says. "That was not so hard." It was the hardest thing you have ever done.

events.text: The full moon comes up over the mountain and you go to meet it the old way, on a grave mound, breathing. But tonight, for the first time in all your years, you do not breathe in. You open your mouth and breathe out, and the bead goes up on your breath, a small full moon going home to the big one, and hangs there between, and the big one looks at it, and sends it back brighter.

choices.text: Breathe it out to the moon on every full moon from now on

effects.log: Every full moon, out and back. The bead comes back each time a little heavier with light, the way a bucket comes up from a deep well. Heaven counts the moon way. It is counting now.

choices.text: Keep it in your mouth. Some things are not lent even to the moon

effects.log: You close your mouth on it. The moon does not mind; it has watched foxes for longer than you. The bead grows anyway, slowly, the clean way. The vixen who bore you would approve, you think, and then think: she did tell you not to let it into another mouth.

events.text: There is one left, or a few. A pale face in an old ledger, a long time ago, in a village that is a market town now. The one you took the breath from is dust. But you can smell their blood still, centuries on: a great-grandchild with the same eyes, coughing in a back room above a cloth shop.

choices.text: Lend the bead to the great-grandchild for a night

effects.log: A cough in the night, a light on a breath, a child well in the morning, centuries late. You strike the line in the ledger in your head. Heaven strikes it in the other ledger, the one that counts.

choices.text: Lend it, and stay a season as the family's physician besides

effects.log: A season as the cheap, odd physician who cures the cough and the mother's knee and the grandfather's temper. When you leave, the family asks your name. You tell them the name of the one you borrowed from, centuries ago. They do not understand. They keep it anyway.

events.text: You go through the Breath ledger one night in your head, the whole of it, every name you borrowed from and every one you gave back, and at the bottom of it there is nothing. Not a line owed. You go through it again to be sure. Nothing. You sit on the grave mound with the moon on you and do not know what to do with your paws.

choices.text: Sit with the empty ledger until dawn

effects.log: It is not lightness exactly. It is the feeling of a debt that is gone, which is a little like grief and a little like the first warm day. At dawn you go down to the paddies and catch a vole, for old times' sake, and let it go.

choices.text: Go and visit the names anyway: the graves, the grandchildren

effects.log: A century of visits. A bow at a grave, a jar of honey on a step, a lantern lit on a bad bend of road. Nobody owes anybody now. That is exactly why it is worth doing.

events.text: The Fox of Heaven. You find out on a clear night when you step off the top of the grave mound and do not come down. The road is under your feet, pale as frost on a dyke, going up. Behind you nine tails of moonlight trail down to the hill like ribbons. On every grave mound in the province, you can feel it, a fox is sitting up and looking at the sky.

choices.text: Walk a little way up, and come back down for now

effects.log: A hundred steps up the moon road, and the province below like a quilt. Then a hundred steps down, and the grass of the mound wet and real under your paws. There is time. For the first time, there is no hurry at all.

choices.text: Go down to the earth under your first mound and lie there a while

effects.log: The earth fell in centuries ago. You lie in the hollow of it anyway, a fox of moonlight in a dip in a millet field, and remember five kits in the dark, and a mother with two tails. Then you get up.

events.text: On the moon road, a little way up, something is caught on the frost at the edge: a folded paper, old, written in a human hand. You know it before you open it. A long time ago, in another life, somebody wrote a poem for a fox, freely, and folded it into the earth of a den. It has come up the road ahead of you, the way a letter goes ahead of a traveller. Smoke round a lonely grave, it says. A coat put off for a plain robe.

choices.text: Read it aloud on the road

effects.log: Your voice on the moon road, reading a human's poem about a fox. It is not a very good poem. It is the best thing anyone has ever given you, and it is on the road ahead of you, and that means somebody, a long time ago, thought you would get this far.

choices.text: Carry it in your mouth beside the bead, unread, the rest of the way

effects.log: Some letters are not for opening on the road. You fold it smaller and carry it with the bead, and it is warm, and it weighs nothing, and it is the only thing you are taking up.

events.text: The top of the road is in sight: the moon, enormous, the colour of a full bead. You have walked a little further each year, and come back down each year, and the grave mounds of the province have got used to a fox of moonlight going up and down over them like a lamp on a stair. Tonight the road does not go down. Tonight it only goes one way.

choices.text: Not yet. Turn round on the road one more time and look at the hills

effects.log: You turn round. The province is below you, asleep: the mounds, the paddies, a wine-house with its lanterns lit, a school with a rice ball on the step. You sit down on the moon road and look at it all night. The moon waits. It has waited for foxes before.

choices.text: Climb

effects.log: You climb. The bead in your mouth goes home into the moon, and you go with it. On the full-moon nights after, foxes in every province sit on the grave mounds and look up, and the oldest of them say, to the kits: that one was a fox, once, like us.

events.text: You dream of the earth under the mound. Not the way you remember it: the way it was. Dark, and warm, and close, four small bodies pushing at you, and the smell of milk, and something old and quiet far above that the soil seems to keep its voice down for. You wake on the mountain with your nine tails stiff with frost, and miss it so much your teeth hurt.

choices.text: Go and find an earth under a grave mound, and lie in its entrance

effects.log: There is a vixen in it with four kits, who looks at you in the entrance with her ears flat and her teeth bare, not afraid at all. You back away and lie in the grass outside all night, guarding it. In the morning she brings you a vole. Professional courtesy.

choices.text: Let the dream go. You are not a kit

effects.log: You shake the frost off and go about the mountain's business. But all that winter, when you sleep, you sleep curled small, with your tails over your nose, the way you did when there were five of you.

events.text: An owl lands in the pine above your mound, a great grey one with eyes like lamps, and looks down at you for a long time. You know owls. An owl took the smallest of the five, in the first year, at the hour when nothing has a shadow. This owl is not that owl. It is a very old owl, though, and it looks at you as if it knew the other one.

choices.text: Ask it, in the small sounds foxes use, whether it remembers

effects.log: Owls do not answer foxes. But it stays on the branch till dawn, and when it goes it leaves a single grey feather on the mound, laid straight, like something that was asked for and given back.

choices.text: Lie still under it until it goes, the way you learned

effects.log: Old as the oldest pine and nine-tailed, and you lie flat under an owl in the grey hour, because a rule is a rule. The owl, you suspect, finds this hilarious. It goes at sunrise. You get up, laughing at yourself a little.

events.text: A voice from the sky, on a night with no moon, which has never happened before. It is not unkind. It says that a fox who has lived as long as you may ask for one thing, once, and be heard. It says it already knows what you will ask. It is waiting to see if it is right.

choices.text: Ask for nothing. You have had a long life, and it is not finished

effects.log: The voice is quiet a long time. Then it says, "I was wrong," sounding pleased about it, and is gone. You sit on the mound in the dark with your tails round your feet and feel, for the first time in centuries, surprising.

choices.text: Ask for the kit an owl took in the first year to have had a long life somewhere

effects.log: "It did," says the voice, after a moment. "In another earth, in another hill. It had eleven kits and died old in a snowdrift, warm." You do not know if it is true. You decide to believe it, and the night is the kindest you have had in a thousand years.

choices.text: Ask to begin again: a blind kit in an earth under a grave mound, remembering everything

effects.log: Dark, and warm, and close. Four small bodies pushing at you from every side, and the smell of milk, and above the soil something old and quiet. Your eyes are not open yet. You remember everything. This time, you think, this time, and fall asleep in the warm middle of the pile.

events.text: Full moon. From the road of cloud you can see every grave mound in the province, and on a great many of them, small and dark against the grass, a fox is sitting up with its face to the sky. Young ones, mostly. One-tailed, two-tailed. One with three, very proud of itself. They are looking at you.

choices.text: Let the moonlight fall a little brighter on the youngest of them

effects.log: Down on a mound in the east a kit no older than a season sits in a pool of light it did not earn, and looks up, astonished. Its bead will start this year. It will not know why. That is how most good things begin.

choices.text: Show them the road: nine tails of light, once, across the sky

effects.log: For one breath the sky has a fan of pale fire in it from horizon to horizon. Every fox in the province goes flat in the grass. Then, one by one, they sit up again, and look harder.

choices.text: Look for the proud three-tailed one, and send it a bad dream about salt peddlers

effects.log: Somewhere a three-tailed fox wakes up shouting and spends the rest of its life crossing the road whenever a man with an A-frame comes along. The vixen who bore you would have approved. It will live a long time.

events.text: {npc}, an immortal sovereign of the upper heavens, has climbed the moon road to the point where it narrows, and stands across it with a staff, and says that it should be closed. "To foxes," {npc} says. "For ever. A road that a thing of masks can walk is a road that a liar can walk. Show me why I am wrong, or turn round."

choices.text: Turn round, and walk down, and come back up behind {npc} as {npc}

effects.log: {npc} turns at a step on the frost and finds their own face looking back, perfectly, down to the scar on the chin, and laughs before they can stop themselves. "Very well," {npc} says. "Point taken. Not closed. Watched."

choices.text: Stand on the road as yourself, and let {npc} look as long as they like

ok.log: {npc} looks all night. In the morning {npc} lowers the staff. "I see a fox," {npc} says. "Only a fox, all the way down. I did not know there were any." The road stays open.

fail.log: {npc} looks all night and sees, as people do, what they came to see. But the road does not close; it was never theirs to close. {npc} goes back up muttering about precedents.

choices.text: Ask {npc} who lied to them

effects.log: It takes a long time to come out. A face, a long time ago, in a life below: someone kind, who was not what they seemed. Not a fox. A person. You sit on the moon road together while {npc} tells it. When it is told, the staff is just a staff.

events.text: You go down the road one night, the whole way, and walk the hill road past the village school at dusk as you did a thousand times. A student is walking it, late, books under one arm, reciting wrong. And a stranger in a pale jacket has fallen into step beside them, at arm's length, with something small and bright held in a closed hand. Another fox, a young one, at the beginning of its story.

choices.text: Walk on the student's other side, and say the old story out loud

effects.log: "There was once a student," you say, "on this road." The young fox looks at you across the student, and goes very still, and then, slowly, opens its hand: the bead is still in it. It falls back into the grass and is gone. The student never knows anything happened.

choices.text: Let the story go the way the young fox chooses

effects.log: You did not get here by being stopped. You go on up the road and leave them to it: a student, a stranger, a bead, a choice. Whatever it chooses, it will have chosen it. That is the only way any fox ever reached the moon.

events.text: There is a table on the terrace of cloud where the four walls of the sky sit, and the centre, and tonight there is a sixth place at it, which there has never been: a mat of plain straw, at the lowest end, for a fox. Round the terrace the four glows burn, blue and white and red and black, and the gold one in the middle. Nobody says anything. The mat says it.

choices.text: Sit at the lowest end, on the straw, and be glad

effects.log: You sit. The storm in the east settles a little. The frost in the west shifts, which might be a tiger making room. The bird in the south sings one note. You have sat at a great many tables in a great many faces. This is the first time in your own.

choices.text: Move the straw mat to the side, and sit on the bare cloud

effects.log: "Too much honour for a fox," you say. The serpent laughs. The north writes it down. In the centre the gold light weighs you once more, like grain, and seems, for a moment, almost amused.

events.text: The mountain is yours now, or you are the mountain's: it comes to the same thing. And a mountain's spirit is prayed to. A hunter is lost on the north face in a snowstorm with a broken bow, and is praying, out loud, very rudely, to whoever is up here. That is you.

choices.text: Walk ahead of the hunter with a light on your tail, down to the valley

effects.log: A pale light in the snow, always a little ahead. The hunter follows it all night, swearing, and walks into the home village at dawn, and goes straight to the shrine with a jar and apologises, at length, for the language.

choices.text: Let the snow stop, for one hour, around the hunter only

effects.log: One hour of still air and starlight in a circle twenty paces wide on the north face, with the storm roaring all round it. The hunter gets the fire lit. The village tells it for generations.

choices.text: Let the hunter find the way alone. A mountain does not carry everyone

effects.log: It is a hard rule, and old, and you keep it. The hunter gets down the mountain three days later with frostbitten toes and a great deal of new respect for mountains. You watch every step of it.

events.text: The villages under your mountain have commissioned a new painting for the shrine: the spirit of the mountain. The painter has come up with brushes and a roll of silk and spent a week sketching the pine, the rocks, the spring, and has left a space in the middle, waiting for the spirit to show itself. The painter, you notice, has been leaving a rice ball by the space every evening.

choices.text: Sit in the space one evening, as you are, black-coated, for the painter

effects.log: The painter sees you, drops the rice ball, picks it up, and paints all night without stopping. The shrine has a black fox in it ever after, under a pine, and the villagers bow to it, and the old ones say it is a strange spirit for a mountain, and the young ones say it suits.

choices.text: Send an old man with a white beard into the painter's dream instead

effects.log: The painting has a white-bearded mountain spirit in it, very correct, very dull. In the corner, small, under the pine, the painter has added a black fox anyway, without being able to say why.

choices.text: Eat the rice ball and leave the space empty

effects.log: The painter waits a week and then paints the empty space as an empty space: pine, rock, spring, and nothing. It is the best painting in the province. People stand in front of it a long time without knowing what they are waiting for.

events.text: A lord from the capital has bought the timber rights to your mountain, all of it, and the woodcutters have come with saws to the old pines, the ones that hold the slope above three villages. You can feel each saw like a tooth being pulled. The headman has written to the lord and been laughed at.

choices.text: Lead the woodcutters astray every night until the lord's money runs out

ok.log: Foxfire in the gullies, paths that loop, tools found up trees. The woodcutters cut eleven pines in a year and go home sure the mountain is haunted. It is. The lord sells the rights at a loss.

fail.log: The foreman is a hard old man who does not follow lights. Forty pines come down before the autumn. You hold the slope above the villages with your own back all winter, and it holds, just. (-10 health)

choices.text: Go to the capital in a geomancer's face and tell the lord the mountain is a dragon vein

effects.log: Cut those pines, you tell the lord, and your family's luck runs out of the hole. The lord, who believes in luck more than in anything, cancels the timber rights by return of post and has a small shrine built on the mountain for safety.

choices.text: Let a few pines go and hold the slope yourself

effects.log: The lord gets his timber. The slope gets you. For years the villages under it sleep safely and never know what is lying across the hill above them in the rain. (-6 health)

events.text: Drought. The villages under the mountain carry the shrine painting down to the threshing floor and pray for rain to it, to you, three days running. You are not a dragon. You cannot make rain. But a mountain's spirit knows where the water is: every spring, every seep, every vein of it under the rock.

choices.text: Open the old spring under the north rock that nobody alive remembers

effects.log: One night of digging with nine black tails for balance, and in the morning water is running down the north gully, clear and cold. The villages call it the fox's spring. They are right.

choices.text: Go east to the dragons' country and ask, once, politely, for rain

ok.log: You stand on the shore of a dragon pool in the east and ask, as a mountain asks. Nothing answers. Three days later a storm comes up from the east, very precisely over your mountain, and stops at its edges. The receipt for it, you suspect, will come later.

fail.log: The pool does not answer foxes, even mountain ones. You go home through the dust, and dig for the old spring after all, and find it. Sometimes the slow way was the only way.

events.text: There is a grave in a village two valleys over that you have never gone to. The bell rang for it in a spring long ago, and you did not let yourself count the strokes. You have kept the long vow since, and kept the mountain, and kept everyone on it you could. Tonight you go, and sit by the grave till dawn.

choices.text: Say the name, which you have never said

effects.log: You say it. Once, and then again, the way the family must have said it. At dawn the grave is a grave, and you are a fox beside it, and something you have carried for centuries is lifted. Not forgotten. Lifted.

choices.text: Sit in silence. Some things are not yours to say

effects.log: You sit till dawn without a word, and go. It is not enough yet. You will come back. The grave will wait; graves are good at it.

events.text: Every spring now, a storm stands over the eastern hills for a day and does not move, blue-green at its heart, and looks at your mountain. It does not rain on you. It does not do anything. It only stands there, the way a creditor stands at a gate. The Azure Dragon has a long memory, and in it is a fox.

choices.text: Go east and stand under the storm, and wait to be spoken to

ok.log: A day and a night under the storm in the rain, saying nothing. At dawn it rains on you once, hard, like a slap, and moves on. You are not forgiven. But you have been, it seems, noticed standing still, and that counts for something in the east.

fail.log: Lightning in the grass beside you, once, close enough to singe all nine tails. A message: not yet. You go home smelling of burnt fur. (-12 health)

choices.text: Mend something of the dragons': a silted spring, a broken pool wall

effects.log: A whole summer clearing a spring in the eastern hills that a young dragon once drank from. You never see a scale. The storm, the next spring, stands a little further off.

choices.text: Ignore it. Foxes and dragons have hated each other since the first pool

effects.log: You turn your back on the east and get on with the mountain. The storm stands there every spring for a century, patient as a stone. The dragons can wait. So, you decide, can you.

events.text: In a dry summer, rain falls on your hill and only on your hill: a narrow grey curtain out of a clear sky, from the east, that waters the pine and the mound and the earth and stops at the edge of the grass. In the morning there is a blue-green scale as big as a rice bowl on the mound, laid there like a calling card.

choices.text: Keep the scale in the earth with your other treasures

effects.log: A scale, nine corks, a feather, a scrap of an old pelt, a headless arrow, if you have them. You lie on them in the dark sometimes and count. It is a fox's whole life, in a hole in a hill.

choices.text: Send something east in return: a fox's thanks

effects.log: You leave a whole pheasant on a rock at the edge of a dragon pool in the east, which is absurd, and know it. The next dry summer the rain comes again. Absurd things are sometimes understood.

events.text: A dragon pool in the next valley, deep and round, where the dragons of the east are said to come down in summer storms. The old foxes always went round it. And the old foxes knew a thing about dragon pools that young foxes did not: the water at the bottom, on a moonless night, is the strongest qi in the land, for one who could drink it without being seen.

choices.text: Go round, as the old foxes did

effects.log: You go round. Some old rules are kept because they are right, and some because nobody has dared to find out, and this is one of the second kind. You keep it anyway.

choices.text: Drink, on a moonless night

ok.log: Cold, heavy, and very strong. The bead in your mouth lights like a coal. Nobody sees. Nobody, you tell yourself. The next summer the storms come down on that valley very hard indeed.

fail.log: Something at the bottom of the pool opens one eye. You do not stay to see the rest. You run three valleys before you stop, and the storm follows you to the second. (-15 health)

events.text: {npc} sits down at your table, where you sit in your borrowed face, and puts a sword on it, which is rude. A grandmaster from the north, with a scar for every decade, who has beaten everyone worth beating and has come south for the one thing left: "The Nine-Tailed Fox," {npc} says. "It lives near here. It wears faces. I mean to duel it. Have you seen it?" You pour {npc} some tea.

choices.text: Send {npc} to the wrong hill, very helpfully

effects.log: "The east hill," you say, "past the shrine. It goes about as an old pedlar." {npc} thanks you gravely, pays for the tea, and is gone for a year. Somewhere in the east, an old pedlar has a very confusing afternoon.

choices.text: Tell {npc} that the fox is not worth fighting: it never fights back

effects.log: "Then I will make it," {npc} says. "Everything fights back, if you push hard enough." You refill the cup. That, you think, is exactly the kind of thing that gets grandmasters led round a marsh for three nights.

choices.text: Offer a friendly bout, here, as the keeper

ok.log: With nothing but a keeper's tricks, the feigned limp and a broom, you hold {npc} to a draw in the yard. {npc} stares at you for a long time. "You fight like a fox," {npc} says. "Everyone in the south does, I suppose."

fail.log: {npc} puts you on the ground in three moves and helps you up, not unkindly. "A keeper should keep to keeping," {npc} says. You agree, with your face in the dust and nine tails held in so hard your back aches. (-12 health)

events.text: {npc} is back at your table, a year older and furious. {npc} has duelled, in order: an old pedlar who was only an old pedlar, a monk who was only a monk, a shrine keeper who turned out to be a very large badger, and a dokkaebi who wanted a rematch. "The fox," {npc} says, "is laughing at me." You pour the tea. It is.

choices.text: Laugh, a little, where {npc} can see

effects.log: {npc} looks at you laughing, and slowly, against every intention, begins to laugh too. It is clearly the first time in years. "The badger," {npc} says, wiping their eyes, "had a very good guard."

choices.text: Suggest {npc} stop looking, and see whether the fox comes

effects.log: "A fox comes to the one who stops chasing," you say. {npc} considers this for a whole cup. "That is either the wisest thing I have heard in the south," {npc} says, "or the stupidest." Both, you think.

events.text: {npc} has stopped looking. Sits at your table every evening now, old, the sword on the floor instead of the table, playing baduk with the carters and losing. Tonight, alone with you after closing, {npc} says without looking up from the board: "It was you. All along. Wasn't it?"

choices.text: Let {npc} see all nine tails, once, in the lamplight, and then duel

ok.log: Nine tails of foxfire in a closed wine-house, and an old grandmaster with a sword, until dawn. You win, barely. {npc} sits on the floor among the overturned stools and laughs until it turns into coughing. "Worth it," {npc} says. "Worth the whole south."

fail.log: Nine tails, a sword, the whole night. At dawn {npc}'s blade is at your throat, and stays there a breath, and is put away. "I wanted to know I could," {npc} says. "Now pour me some tea." (-15 health)

choices.text: Say yes, and pour the tea, and do not fight

effects.log: {npc} nods, and moves a stone on the board, and says, "Good. I am too old now anyway." You play until the lamp goes out. {npc} wins, for once. You may have let it happen. You will never say.

choices.text: Say no, and mean it kindly

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long moment and then down at the board again. "No," {npc} agrees. "Of course not." You both know. It is the most polite lie either of you has ever told.

events.text: {npc} is a master of the highest realm, the kind there are three of in a generation, and has been drinking at your table all week in a plain coat, saying nothing. Tonight {npc} puts the cup down. "I can see every face you have worn," {npc} says, "stacked like paper. Thirty, forty. I am curious. Which one is yours?"

choices.text: Answer honestly: none of them, and all of them

effects.log: "That is the right answer," {npc} says, "for a fox. Is it the right answer for you?" You do not know. {npc} pours you a cup, which is how masters say: think about it.

choices.text: Show {npc} the first one: a red-brown fox kit in an earth under a mound

effects.log: For one breath, across the table, a blind kit with milk on its nose. {npc} smiles for the first time all week. "Ah," {npc} says. "That one. Yes. Keep that one somewhere safe."

choices.text: Ask {npc} the same question back

effects.log: {npc} opens their mouth, closes it, and laughs. "A disciple's face," {npc} says at last. "A master's. A widow's. A killer's, once. I have more than you think." You drink to it. Everyone does.

events.text: {npc} comes back years later, much older, and sits at the same table, and before ordering anything asks: "Well? Did you find it?"

choices.text: "I think it is the one that keeps asking"

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly. "Then you have one," {npc} says. "Most people never notice it." You drink to it, the two of you, until the lamp burns down.

choices.text: "Not yet. Come back in a hundred years"

effects.npcPass: old age, years later, still curious
effects.log: "I will not be here," {npc} says, cheerfully. "Tell my grave." You do, a hundred years later, standing by a plain stone on a mountain. The grave takes it well.

events.text: {npc}, an envoy of the court above the clouds, has come down to audit the Breath ledger of every fox in the land, and has taken a room at your wine-house to do it, with a scroll so long it trails out of the door. {npc} does not look up when you bring the tea. "Sit," {npc} says. "You are on page four thousand."

choices.text: Sit, and answer every line truly

effects.log: Borrowed: this one, that one. Given back: this one, that one. Still owed: this one. {npc} writes without comment. At the end {npc} looks up for the first time. "Correct," {npc} says. "Nobody is ever correct."

choices.text: Ask to see the page before the envoy reads it

effects.log: {npc} considers the request as if it were a legal question, which it is, and turns the scroll round. Your page. Every breath, in a clerk's perfect hand. It is much shorter than you feared, or much longer. It depends which column you read first.

choices.text: Ask how many foxes have ever had an empty page

effects.log: "Eleven," {npc} says, "in four thousand pages." A pause. "Most of them never left the hill. It is not hard to owe nothing if you never meet anyone." You think about that for a long time.

events.text: {npc}, the envoy, has finished auditing four provinces and stops at your wine-house on the way back up, with the scroll rolled very tight. "Your page," {npc} says, over tea. "I have a note to add to it. Is there anything you want me to write down before I do?"

choices.text: "Write that I am still paying"

effects.log: {npc} writes it. "Still paying," {npc} reads back. "That is a better line than most foxes get." The scroll goes up the mountain with your sentence on it.

choices.text: "Write that the page is empty, and that it was not easy"

effects.log: {npc} writes: empty; not easy. Then, after a moment, underlines the second part. You have never seen a clerk of heaven underline anything. It may be the highest compliment the court above the clouds pays.

choices.text: "Write that the fox made good tea"

effects.log: {npc} looks at you over the cup for a long time, and then writes it. It is in the ledger still, on page four thousand, in a perfect clerk's hand: made good tea.

events.text: {npc}, a heavenly immortal, has come down to your table, and looks at you with a geomancer's eyes, the kind that see the earth to the bottom. "In a life I barely remember," {npc} says, "I was a student on a hill road, and a stranger walked beside me every evening, and one evening I swallowed something, and fell, and looked at the ground. I have been looking at it ever since. I think it was yours."

choices.text: "It was. You did exactly what the schoolmaster said"

effects.log: {npc} laughs, a long time. "I always wondered if I should have fallen the other way," {npc} says. "The sky." You tell {npc} that nobody ever does. That is the point of the story. Nobody ever does.

choices.text: "I am glad it went to someone who used it"

effects.log: "Every good grave site in three provinces," {npc} says. "Every spring, every vein. Two hundred villages that never flooded." A pause. "I would like to say thank you to the fox. I never could, before." Now you have.

events.text: {npc} has a furnace in a back lane and a theory: a nine-tailed fox's bead, ground fine and taken with cinnabar on the ninth day of the ninth month, makes an elixir of a thousand years. {npc} explains this to you at length over a bowl of your soup, not knowing whose soup it is. "I only need to find the fox," {npc} says, "and convince it."

choices.text: Ask what {npc} would do with a thousand years

effects.log: {npc} starts to answer three times and stops three times. "Finish the work," {npc} says at last. "Whatever the work turns out to be." You have lived longer than any elixir promises. You tell {npc} the work never turns out to be anything, and that is the best of it.

choices.text: Tell {npc}, gently, that the fox would never agree

effects.log: "Everyone agrees to something," says {npc}. "I will find what the fox wants." You admire the confidence. You lock your door that night anyway.

choices.text: Lead {npc} on a chase for a fox bead that is only a river pearl

effects.log: A year of rumours, maps and a pearl-diver's widow. {npc} comes back with a river pearl, grinds it with cinnabar on the ninth day of the ninth month, drinks it, and gets a stomach ache of a thousand years. Mostly a week.

events.text: The furnace in the back lane has exploded, again, and {npc} is sitting in the ruins with singed eyebrows and a real grief: a younger sibling with a wasting cough that no physician can touch. That is what the elixir was for. It was always for that. {npc} tells you this over your soup, not looking up.

choices.text: Lend the bead to the sibling for a night, as a stranger

effects.log: A stranger comes to the sickroom at night with a small light, and in the morning the cough is gone, and the stranger too. {npc} closes the furnace for good and opens an herb stall instead. It is a much better use of a back lane.

choices.text: Teach {npc} real medicine instead of elixirs

effects.log: Willow bark, ginger, a long winter of careful nursing. The sibling lives. Not because of you, exactly; because {npc} sat up every night and did the work. That is the elixir. It always was.

events.text: {npc} keeps the herb stall in the back lane now, old, with a sign over it that says nothing about elixirs. On the shelf behind the counter, where anyone else would keep an ancestral tablet, there is a small clay fox with nine tails, very badly made. "For luck," {npc} says, when you ask. "And for a stranger."

choices.text: Buy something you do not need, and pay too much

effects.log: Ginger, three measures. {npc} gives you the change exactly, and a fourth measure free, and looks at you over the counter a moment too long. Neither of you says anything. The clay fox looks very pleased with itself.

choices.text: Mend the clay fox's broken ear while {npc} is not looking

effects.log: In the morning the clay fox has two good ears and {npc} stands in front of the shelf for a long time with both hands over their mouth. The stall is lucky after that. Everybody in the lane can tell you so.

events.text: First snow, and the fox hunters are out: twenty men, dogs, two falcons, and a bounty board's worth of rice talking in all of them. They have your tracks. Nine tails leave a very particular track in fresh snow.

choices.text: Lead them round the mountain with foxfire until dark

ok.log: Round and round, lights in the pines, tracks that go up a tree and stop. At dark the hunters build a fire and argue. In the morning they go home with a story instead of a pelt.

fail.log: One falcon is not fooled by lights. It stoops on you twice before you get under the rocks. You lie there all day with the dogs baying above and come out at moonrise, bleeding. (-12 health)

choices.text: Turn and face the dogs on the ridge

ok.log: Nine tails open on the ridge like a fan of fire, and the dogs sit down in the snow, all of them, at once, and will not get up. The hunters carry them home. The bounty goes up.

fail.log: Too many dogs, too much snow. You get off the ridge with a bite in your flank and an arrow through the fur of one tail. (-15 health)

choices.text: Go to ground under the oldest mound you know and wait

effects.log: Three days under the earth with your tails over your nose while the dogs go back and forth above. On the fourth they give up. It is not glorious. It is how foxes get old.

events.text: A young hunter has joined the parties this year who is very good: patient, quiet, reads the snow like a book, and never once follows a light. {npc} has found your earth three times and left it alone three times, which no hunter has ever done. On the fourth, {npc} sits down by the entrance and waits.

choices.text: Come out and sit opposite {npc}

effects.log: Nine tails and a bow, a pace apart in the snow. Neither moves for an hour. Then {npc} nods, unstrings the bow, and goes home. Next winter {npc} leads the parties to every hill but yours.

choices.text: Leave by the back way, and leave {npc} a pheasant at the front

effects.log: {npc} finds the pheasant, laughs out loud in the empty snow, and takes it home. It is, you suspect, the beginning of a long and very careful friendship.

choices.text: Lead {npc} far into the mountains and lose them there

ok.log: Three days. {npc} follows every true track and none of the false ones, and still comes out on the wrong side of the mountain. "Next year," {npc} says to the trees, cheerfully.

fail.log: {npc} is not lost. {npc} is waiting for you at the pass, with an arrow on the string, and lets it go into the snow at your feet. A warning. (-10 health)

events.text: A rumour in three provinces: the nine-tailed fox is a white fox now, and a white pelt would buy a county. Trappers come up the valleys with iron jaws and good bait. The village under your hill hides its children's snares in the woodpile, out of loyalty, and sends the trappers up the wrong path.

choices.text: Spring every trap on the mountain in one night

effects.log: Forty traps, forty sticks, forty iron mouths snapped shut on nothing. The trappers find them in the morning in a neat row by the road. They go home. They will be back.

choices.text: Thank the village, in a face: rice for every house

effects.log: Every house in the village finds a sack of rice on the step one winter morning, and nobody asks where from. The trappers go up the wrong path again the next year, and the next.

events.text: A dog at the door. A new one, yellow, belonging to the neighbour's new son-in-law, and it has decided on its first night that your house is the most important thing in the lane. It barks at your gate until dawn, every night, and the lane is starting to wonder why.

choices.text: Win the dog over, slowly, with scraps and patience

ok.log: A month of scraps through the gate. The dog stops barking and starts sleeping on your step instead, which the lane finds hilarious and entirely normal.

fail.log: Some dogs cannot be bought. This one takes the scraps and barks anyway, louder, as if insulted. The lane's wondering goes on.

choices.text: Hide the tails harder: no lamp after dark

effects.log: A dark house, an early bed, the long way round the lane. The dog barks at nothing for a week and then, bored, at the son-in-law.

choices.text: Look the dog in the eye, once, as what you are

effects.log: One look over the gate, nine tails' worth. The dog lies down, whimpers, and never barks at your gate again, though it watches your shadow very carefully for the rest of its life.

events.text: A full moon in company. The neighbours have dragged a table out into the yard for the harvest moon and set your place at it, and there is no excuse left that you have not used. The moon comes up enormous over the paddies. Nine tails ache behind you like a held breath.

choices.text: Sit with your back to a wall and the moon behind the roof

effects.log: Rice wine, songs, a grandmother's story about a fox. Your shadow falls on the wall behind you, and the wall is in shadow too. Nobody sees. Nobody, at least, says.

choices.text: Pour for everyone, all night, so nobody looks at you

effects.log: A host is invisible. You keep every cup full until the moon is down, and the neighbours remember it as the best harvest night in years, and cannot quite remember whether you were there.

choices.text: Plead a fever and go in early

effects.log: "Every full moon," says somebody behind you, not quite quietly enough, "a fever." You close the door. Your tails come out all at once, like a sigh.

events.text: The matchmaker of the county comes to your gate with a red cloth bundle and a list: a family with land, a widowed scholar, a merchant's second child, all very suitable for the person you are pretending to be. The matchmaker has never failed. The matchmaker has also never met a nine-tailed fox.

choices.text: Decline, politely, with a story about a vow to an old parent

effects.log: A vow to a dying parent, very touching. The matchmaker wipes an eye and goes away, and comes back next year with a longer list. Matchmakers are the most patient creatures on earth after foxes.

choices.text: Find a match for the matchmaker instead

effects.log: It takes you a summer. The matchmaker is furious, then flustered, then married. The county agrees it was the match of the decade, and nobody ever brings you a list again.

choices.text: Ask about each family, closely, and send help where it is needed

effects.log: The family with land is in debt. The widowed scholar cannot afford ink. The merchant's child wants to be a physician. You marry nobody, and by spring three households are a little better off and never know why.

events.text: A child in the lane, five years old and fearless, comes into your yard while you are hanging washing and says, very loudly: "My grandmother says you have tails. Can I see them?" Three neighbours stop what they are doing.

choices.text: Laugh, and say every grown-up has tails, they only hide them

effects.log: The neighbours laugh too. The child goes home and asks every grown-up in the lane to show their tails, and by evening the whole lane is laughing at the grandmother instead of looking at you.

choices.text: Show the child one, very small, behind the washing

effects.log: One tail, for a breath, behind a hanging quilt. The child's eyes go perfectly round. "I will not tell," the child whispers, and does not, ever, and grows up to be the kind of person nobody can make tell anything.

choices.text: Give the child a persimmon and change the subject

effects.log: Persimmons are stronger than grandmothers. The child goes off chewing and forgets the question for a whole year.

events.text: A lamp in the next room, and your shadow on the paper door between. You feel it a moment too late: the shadow has more behind it than a person should. Out in the lane a passer-by has stopped, and is looking at your door, and is very still.

choices.text: Blow the lamp out and sit in the dark until they go

effects.log: Dark. A long silence in the lane. Footsteps, at last, going on, a little faster than before. By morning it will be a story. Stories are not proof. Yet.

choices.text: Step out of the door at once, a person, and greet them

effects.log: "A cold night," you say, and the passer-by says it is, and looks past you at the door, where the lamp now throws only one shadow, yours, ordinary. They decide they were tired. Most people do.

choices.text: Let them see. Nine tails on a paper door: let the story be a good one

effects.log: You lift all nine, slowly, on the paper, like a fan. Out in the lane someone sits down hard in the mud. Within a week three villages tell it, and every telling is wrong in a different way.

events.text: A salt peddler on the hill road at dusk, with an A-frame on the back and a forked stick to prop it, walking like someone who is never in a hurry and never lost. The second of the three rules you learned as a kit, a very long time ago. Nine tails, and your fur still goes up.

choices.text: Go flat in the grass, the way she taught you

effects.log: The peddler passes. The stick swings. You lie in the silver grass with your heart going like a kit's and feel, absurdly, centuries younger.

choices.text: Walk down and buy salt, in a face, to see if the peddler knows

ok.log: A measure of coarse salt and a nod. The peddler does not know, or does not say. You carry the salt home and pour a little on your doorstep, which is supposed to keep foxes out. It does not work. You are oddly disappointed.

fail.log: The peddler weighs the salt, hands it over, and lets the stick fall, very gently, across your path as you turn. A message. You step over it. Behind you the peddler says, "Hm."

events.text: Foxfire weather: a soft autumn night with the marsh steaming. On the road below there is a drunk, a lost child, and a pair of bandits, none of whom know the others are there. You have lights enough for all three.

choices.text: The child first: a light to the gate, all the way

effects.log: A light on your tail, always just ahead, to the village gate. The child goes in. Nobody believes the child. They never do. The child remembers for life.

choices.text: The bandits: round the same hill till dawn

effects.log: At sunrise the bandits sit down by the road where they started, and look at each other, and give up banditry for a farm in the next province. Possibly.

choices.text: The drunk: home, singing, by the long way

effects.log: You walk ahead with a light, and the drunk follows it, singing the wrong words to every song, all the way to a gate where someone is waiting with a lamp and a temper.

events.text: A knock at the gate. {npc} stands there, thin and tired and polite, with a bundle on one shoulder: the grandchild of someone who went pale, a long time ago, after a stranger stayed the season. "They say the family has a weakness of the chest," {npc} says. "They say it began with a fox. I came to ask if you know anything about it. Everyone says you know everything."

choices.text: Lend the bead to {npc} for a night, and say nothing about why

effects.log: A night's lodging, a light on a breath while {npc} sleeps. In the morning {npc} breathes all the way down for the first time in years, and goes home puzzled and well. One less line in the ledger.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the truth, and then lend it

ok.log: {npc} listens to all of it, white-faced, and then says: "Then fix it." You do. In the morning {npc} goes home well, and tells the family a story that nobody believes, and lights a candle for the fox every year anyway.

fail.log: {npc} backs out of the gate halfway through and runs. The lane hears about it by noon. You will have to find the family another way, later, in another face.

events.text: A student on the hill road at dusk, reciting the Thousand Characters wrong, with books in a cloth under one arm. They walk past your mound every evening. Every fox on every hill knows this story. It is still a long road, and the student is still alone on it.

choices.text: Walk behind at a distance, as a light in the grass, till the school

effects.log: A small light in the silver grass, all the way to the school gate, and the student never quite sees it. Heaven is dark, earth is yellow. You correct the recitation in your head every step.

choices.text: Leave a rice ball on the school step, for once the other way round

effects.log: Nobody ever left you one, under that floor. Tonight the student finds one waiting, and eats it, and does not know who to thank. That is exactly right.

events.text: A shaman at a village rite, fan in one hand and bells in the other, turns in the middle of a dance and looks straight into the dark at the edge of the yard, where you are, and stops. The drums stop. Everyone looks. The shaman says, quite calmly: "You. Not tonight."

choices.text: Bow, from the dark, and go

effects.log: The drums start again behind you. Some old courtesies are older than you, and you keep them. The shaman, you notice, leaves a cup of rice wine on the wall at the edge of the yard after the rite.

choices.text: Step into the light, as you are, and ask: "When, then?"

effects.log: Nine tails in the torchlight, and a whole village frozen. The shaman considers you, and the question, for a long time. "When you are finished," the shaman says, and goes back to the dance.

events.text: A year of the vow, and the test comes as it always comes, small and close. {npc}, the ferry-keeper, with a laugh like a barrel rolling, has fallen asleep at your table after closing. The breath of a strong sleeper is warm and deep, and you are nine-tailed, and tired, and the bead in your mouth is a little dimmer than you would like.

choices.text: Open the window, put a blanket over {npc}, and sit by the cold till dawn

effects.log: All night by an open window, with a warm sleeper across the room. At dawn {npc} wakes, thanks you for the blanket, and goes off whistling to the ferry. The days go on adding up.

choices.text: Wake {npc} and send them home

effects.log: "Home," you say, "before your family sends the dogs." {npc} goes, grumbling. You bolt the door and sit with your back against it. Some temptations are best answered with a bolt.

choices.text: One breath. Only one

effects.log: One thread of breath, and the bead brightens like a coal. {npc} is pale at breakfast and blames the drink. The vow breaks. The moon does not say anything. It does not need to.

events.text: {npc}, a rich man's steward, insults your face in the street in front of the whole market: says you cheat everyone you deal with, says your family were nobody, says it loudly, for the pleasure of it. In all the centuries foxes have done worse for less, in the old way, which the stories name and this one will not.

choices.text: Let it go. The market is watching the steward, not you

effects.log: You weigh the next customer's rice exactly, in silence. The market watches {npc} shout at nobody, and slowly begins to laugh, and {npc} goes home red to the ears. The days go on adding up.

choices.text: Lead {npc} into the paddy with foxfire that night: humiliation, not harm

effects.log: {npc} spends the night up to the waist in the deep paddy, following lights, and walks into the market at dawn soaked and silent. Not harm. Very nearly not. The moon, you think, will let it pass. It does.

choices.text: Follow {npc} home in the dark

effects.log: You follow, and stop at the gate, and do not go in. But the following was enough: the vow was never only about what you do. You feel it break in your mouth like a thin shell. You go home. {npc} sleeps soundly, never knowing.

events.text: In the market, on a fur-seller's pole, among the marten and the badger: a fox pelt, red-brown, with one white forepaw. Very old. Kept a long time in a chest. The fur-seller, {npc}, sees you looking and names a price, and says, cheerfully, that the old ones are the best, and that there is a nine-tailed one on the hill above town that would fetch a fortune.

choices.text: Buy the pelt, take it to the hill, and bury it under a mound

effects.log: You pay without bargaining, which makes {npc} suspicious, and carry the pelt up the hill in your arms like something asleep. You bury it in an earth under an old grave mound, where it should have been all along. The days go on adding up.

choices.text: Walk away. Hold the vow with both hands

effects.log: You walk away from the pole with your jaw shut so hard it aches. Behind you {npc} calls the price lower, and lower. You do not turn round. (-5 health)

choices.text: Come back that night for {npc}

effects.log: You come back at night and wreck the stall, every pole, every pelt, and the fur-seller runs into the dark screaming about foxes. Nobody is hurt. It does not matter. The vow breaks on the first pole.

events.text: A lamp, a paper door, a shadow with nine tails in it, and a scream. Then the dogs, and the lane, and the lamps coming. In the yard {npc}, who has known your face for years, is standing perfectly still with a hand over their mouth, looking at the door, and then at you, as you come out of it.

choices.text: Stop in the yard, and say one true thing to {npc} before you go

effects.log: "I was kind to you," you say, "because I wanted to be. Not because of anything." {npc} takes the hand away from their mouth. The dogs are at the gate. You go over the wall. Behind you, {npc} tells the lane you went the other way.

choices.text: Go over the wall without a word

effects.log: Over the wall, through the persimmon orchard, up the hill road. By dawn you are three valleys away. Behind you a whole life you kept for years is a story the lane tells about a fox, and {npc} is in it.

choices.text: Lead the dogs off with foxfire, away from {npc}'s house

ok.log: Lights in the paddies, three ways at once. The dogs and the lamps go after all of them. {npc}'s house is quiet by midnight. Nobody blames {npc} for anything, which was the point.

fail.log: One dog follows you, not the lights, and catches your hind leg at the wall. You get away. The lane does not. They question {npc} for a week. (-12 health)

events.text: Some time after your face fell, {npc} walks up the hill road to your mound with a bundle in both arms and puts it down on the grass. Your old things, from the house: a cup, a quilt, the good knife. "You left these," {npc} says, to the grass. "I thought you would want them."

choices.text: Come out of the grass, as you are

effects.log: Nine tails in daylight, a pace away. {npc} looks at them for a long time and then sits down on the mound. "I always wondered why you never got cold," {npc} says. You both laugh, which surprises both of you.

choices.text: Stay hidden, and leave something in return on the mound

effects.log: The next morning there is a small glowing stone on the mound where the bundle was. {npc} takes it home. The house has no fevers for a generation.

events.text: The face falls in the worst way: in front of {npc}, the one person in that life you would have told, eventually, yourself. There is no scream. {npc} only says, very quietly, "Oh," and sits down on the step, and puts the lamp down carefully so it will not spill.

choices.text: Sit down on the step beside {npc}

effects.log: You sit. Neither of you says anything for a long time. The lamp burns. In the lane the dogs have started up, but they are a long way off. "You should go," {npc} says at last. "Come back, though." You will.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to tell the lane it was a dream

ok.log: {npc} goes out into the lane in a nightrobe and tells the gathering lamps that it was a nightmare, a cat, a shadow, too much wine. It is not a good lie. It is told so firmly that it works.

fail.log: {npc} tries, and cannot get the words out. The lamps come in at the gate. You are gone before the first dog. {npc} is still sitting on the step when they arrive, saying nothing at all.

events.text: In the morning the bead does not come back. {npc} swallowed it in the night, half-asleep, the way the old stories always say, and now sits on the floor with both hands over their chest where a faint light shows through the cloth, staring at the hills through the window as if they had never seen earth before. Half your light is in them. A tail has folded flat against your back like a broken fan.

choices.text: Sit down with {npc} and ask for it back, and wait

ok.log: You talk until noon: the earth they can see, what it will cost you, what it would cost them to keep. In the end {npc} leans over and gives it back on a breath, freely. The folded tail opens. {npc} keeps the memory of the earth. That, you cannot take.

fail.log: {npc} is too frightened to listen, and runs out of the door with your light in them. You let them go. You will find them again. The old tales are clear: it has to be given.

choices.text: Let {npc} keep it, and go on diminished

effects.log: "Keep it," you say. "Look at the earth with it. Do some good." {npc} becomes, in time, a geomancer the whole province trusts. You go on, slower, with a folded tail, and look for the bead's light in the world instead of in your mouth.

choices.text: Take it back the old way

effects.npcDie: a sudden sickness in the night, which the village called a fox's sickness
effects.log: The old way, which the stories name and this one will not. In the morning there is a funeral in the village, and your tail is open again, and the bead is in your mouth, and it is very bright, and it is not the same bead it was.

events.text: Years after the bead went into another mouth, {npc} is a famous geomancer in three provinces, never wrong about a grave site, and has come back to your hill with a compass on a cord. "I can see where every vein of qi runs," {npc} says to the grass. "Except one. There is a vein that runs from this mound straight up into the sky, and I cannot see where it goes. I think it is yours. I think I am in the way."

choices.text: Ask for the bead, now, freely

ok.log: {npc} gives it back on a breath, sitting on the mound, with a face like someone setting down a heavy jar. "I still see the earth," {npc} says afterwards, surprised. Of course. Some things stay.

fail.log: {npc} cannot do it. Not yet. "Next spring," {npc} says, ashamed, and goes. You believe it. Next spring is a long way off for a human, and very near for a fox.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to keep it till the end of that life, and then give it to the hill

effects.log: {npc} keeps it for the rest of a long life and does nothing but good with it. On the last day, very old, {npc} is carried up to your mound and breathes it out onto the grass, and you are there.

events.text: {npc}, a minister's clerk on the long road home in disgrace, drinks alone at your table and talks to the cup. "Twenty years at court," {npc} says, "and the one thing I learned is that the best advice in the palace always came from someone nobody could later find. A physician. A secretary. Gone the year after. Like a fox." {npc} looks up. "You have that look, you know."

choices.text: Laugh, and ask what look that is

effects.log: "The look of someone who has heard everything twice," {npc} says, and laughs too, and the moment passes. In the morning {npc} leaves an extra coin on the table and a note: whoever you were at court, thank you.

choices.text: Give {npc} the advice the palace never did: go home and plant something

effects.log: {npc} goes home and plants persimmons, and in a few years sends you a basket every autumn with no name on it. The best advice, as {npc} said, always comes from someone nobody can later find.

events.text: {npc}, a child of eight who helps in the kitchen, sits on the step after closing and demands a story, any story, but a true one. "Grandmother's are all made up," {npc} says. "Yours sound like you were there."

choices.text: Tell the one about the five kits in the earth under the grave mound

effects.log: Dark, and warm, and five of you, and an owl, and a mother with two tails. {npc} falls asleep before the end, which is just as well, because you have never been sure how it ends.

choices.text: Tell the one about the student on the hill road, and the bead

effects.log: {npc} listens with eyes like saucers. "And did the student look at the sky?" Nobody ever does, you say. {npc} decides to be the first. You hope, very much, that {npc} gets the chance.

choices.text: Tell a made-up one, so the child keeps believing grandmother

effects.log: A tiger, a persimmon, a frightened thief. {npc} laughs, says it is a grandmother story after all, and goes to bed satisfied. Some truths can wait until a child is older. Some can wait for centuries.

events.text: {npc}, a famous swordsman of the orthodox sects, sits at your table every spring on the way to the capital, and has done for many years, and has never once asked how old you are. Tonight, grey now, {npc} raises a cup. "To the keeper," {npc} says, "who has not aged a day. I will not ask. I only want you to know I noticed."

choices.text: Raise a cup back: "To the guest who never asked"

effects.log: You drink to each other. {npc} keeps coming every spring until the springs stop, and never asks, and the last time, leaving, puts a hand on the paper door, very gently, where your shadow is, as if saying goodbye to both of you.

choices.text: Answer the question that was not asked

effects.log: "More years than the sects have had names," you say, "give or take." {npc} nods slowly, as if that were exactly the number. "Then I am a child at your table," {npc} says. "Good. I always felt like one here."
